-the great importance of Manchuria in the economic development of Japan. Nor do we consider unreasonable her demand for the establishment of a stable government which would be capable of maintaining the order necessary for the economic development of the country. There is no question-
-declares the report-
-of returning to the conditions before September, 1931. A satisfactory regime for the future might be evolved out of the present one without any violent change. . . .
It is impossible not to realize that, at the heart of the problem for Japan, lies her anxiety concerning the political development of modern China, and the future to which it is tending.
And as to China, the report declares that all her " claims should be subordinated to this one dominating need for the effective internal reconstruction of the state."
Nevertheless, so long as the existing chaotic conditions prevail in China, it is indeed difficult to find a solution of China's difficulties with other nations by applying the terms of the League Covenant, the Washington Treaty and the Kellogg Peace Pact, which are applicable to thoroughly organized and responsible national governments rather than to a

Sino-Japanese Dispute-Mr. Cahan
politically disorganized Asiatic state, some of whose leaders are evidently actuated by a belief that, under the protection of the international agreements, to which their country is a party, they may persist in hostile and provocative acts against foreigners without fear of retaliation.
Article 10 of the League of Nations has been the subject of considerable discussion in this country. That article reads as follows:
The members of the league undertake to respect and preserve, as against external aggression, the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all members of the league. In ease of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression, the council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
It is well known that at the conference at Paris, which framed the treaty of Versailles, Sir Robert Borden, then Prime Minister of Canada and senior Canadian delegate to that conference, took strong exception to the terms of this article 10.
Subsequently at the fourth assembly of the league, which was held at Geneva in September, 1923, the 'Canadian delegation sought to repeal article 10, or to amend it so as to provide that "no member shall be under the obligation to engage in any act of war without the consent of its parliament, legislative or other representative body."
The committee which considered the Canadian amendment reported in favour of the following interpretative resolution:
The assembly, desirous of defining the scope of the obligations contained in article 10 of the covenant so far as regards the points raised by the delegation of Canada, adopts the following resolution:

"It is in conformity with the spirit of article 10 that in the event of the council considering it to be its duty to recommend the application of military measures in consequetnice of an aggression or danger or threat of aggression, the council shall be bound to take account, more particularly, of the geographical situation and of the special conditions of each state.
" It is for the constitutional authorities of each member to decide, in reference' to the obligation of preserving the independence and the integrity of the territory of members, in what degree the member is bound to assure the execution of this obligation by employment of its military forces.
"The recommendations made by the council shall be regarded as being of the highest importance and shall be taken into consideration by all the members of the league with the desire to execute their engagements in good faith."
This resolution failed to obtain the unanimous approval of the fourth assembly; twenty-nine states voting therefor, Persia voting "No" and thirteen states abstaining from voting. Therefore this resolution has no binding effect.
I deemed it expedient at the special assembly in December last to refer to Canada's now historic point of view, inasmuch as it was then evident that there were delegates from some of the recently organized states of Europe, who foresee that coming events may place their own state boundaries in jeopardy, and who were disposed to press for an arbitrary condemnation of Japan and the premature enforcement, in their interests, of the sanctions prescribed by the provisions of article 16.
I would like to suggest that one occupying the position I did, representing Canada and standing before that assembly of representatives from all parts of the world, must necessarily feel a great responsibility indeed, in view of the fact that to attain the ultimate end sought by many of the delegates might have involved placing upon Canada the responsibility of again sending her military forces into the far east for the preservation of peace in Manchuria. And knowing as I did, the historic development of opinion in Canada with regard to article 10, I conceived it my bounden duty to state to that assembly what I believed to be the prevailing public opinion in Canada which has been accepted and endorsed by each successive government in our country, in order that there might be no misapprehension as to the position which I as a delegate of Canada was then taking.
Article 16 would involve:
The severance of all trade or financial relations, the prohibition of all intercourse between their nationals and the nationals of the covenant breaking state, and the prevention of all financial, commercial or personal intercourse between the nationals of the covenant breaking state and the nationals of any other state, whether a member of the league or not.
I think that I truly interpreted the opinion of this government and of this parliament, in suggesting that the time had not then arrived for the adoption of such extreme measures. I believe that the views of the governments of the British commonwealth of nations were expressed in an editorial of The Times, of London, on January 24 last:
And there must be very few among the responsible ministers who have been watching, waiting, and deliberating upon events in Manchuria who can have much doubt that a policy of active intervention would almost certainly have produced far more catastrophic results than the passing of three or four Manchurian provinces under the direction of Japan. League action could only be effective if, on the facts of the dispute, as found impartially by its own agents, one disputant or another were adjudged to be wholly in the wrong, and if the volume of condemnatory opinion were strong enough in a sufficient number of countries to make the governments of those countries ready to sacrifice human

Sino-Japanese Dispute-Mr. Cahan
lives, material, trade, and money in taking action against tlie "aggressor." Threats of action by the league in any other circumstances would be no more than a bluff. The requisite [DOT]conditions for action have certainly not existed in the case of the Sino-Japanese dispute.
The league therefore has very properly confined itself in this case to a policy of conciliation; and, in view of the temporary refusal of the two parties to the dispute to be reconciled, all that it can do now is to draw up the lines of a settlement which in its opinion would be at once feasible and just. . . .
It is at any rate certain that it is no part of the duty of the states in the league, whether collectively or individually, to pass moral judgment upon one or other of its members. Their business is to devise a solution which is likely to be practicable in the near or distant future, and which is in consonance with the principles of the league.
Informed and dispassionate public opinion in the neighbouring republic finds expression in an editorial of the New York Times, of February 22nd last, from which I quote:
No fair-minded person can deny that Japan has rights in Manchuria and a good case to argue. In the statement of it made on Tuesday by the Japanese delegation at Geneva, there is a great deal of force. One strong consideration in favour of the Japanese contention has all along been admitted. This is that there has been no well-organized and stable and continuing Chinese government with which a foreign nation can make agreements. When the covenant of the League of Nations speaks of a country made the victim of aggressive action, it manifestly intends a cohesive and recognized government able to maintain law and order within its own boundaries and to speak for the wishes of its subjects and citizens. This has not been the ease with China since the overthrow of the monarchy at Peking. Other nations, including the United States, have been embarrassed and baffled by this lack of a central Chinese authority, but it is doubtless true that Japan, in her more intimate relations, has felt the awkwardness of the Chinese situation more keenly. In fairness, let it be admitted that Japan has had real complaints and grievances in Manchuria.
The New York Times continues as follows: The league has been considerate. In this whole matter of the dispute between China and Japan it has been most cautious and considerate -many have thought too much so. Even now it will not be precipitate in pronouncing judgment. It is willing to give Japan still more time to find a way to accept some plan of conciliation and peaceful adjustment. What the Japanese people should understand, what the Japanese government should perceive, is that those who through the years have been most friendly to [DOT]Japan are to-day the ones who most strongly desire that she make, if need be, some minor sacrifices of prestige in order to win back the cordial^ reception of her as one full worthy of being included in the sisterhood of modern and peace-loving nations.
The address which I made on the Sino-Japanese question on December 8, 1932, be-rMr. Cahan.]
fore the special assembly of the league, has been criticized on several occasions in Canada by those who had evidently not carefully studied the Lytton report. Notwithstanding their criticisms, I have reason to believe that that address was widely approved by eminent delegates from several of the leading states there assembled, that its delivery did not, in any measure, detract from the reputation which Canada had previously acquired at the league assemblies, but that, in part at least, it influenced the league's decision to increase the number of its committee of nineteen, and to give to Canada, as a state adjacent to the Pacific ocean, permanent representation on that committee. Now after having read over the verbatim report of that address, I have no desire to amend or modify the views which I then expressed, which I believe to be consistent with the report of the Lytton commission and in accord with predominate political opinion throughout the British commonwealth.
The assembly of the league, at which I attended, after discussion of the Lytton report, adopted, on December 9th, 1932, the following resolution, in favour of which I recorded the vote of Canada:
The assembly, having received the report of the commission of inquiry set up under the resolution adopted on December 10, 1931, by the council, together with the observations of the parties and the minutes of the council meetings held from November 21 to 28, 1932, in view of the discussions which took place at its meetings from December 6 to 9, 1932, requests the special committee appointed under its resolution of March 11, 1932:
(1)	To study the report of the commission of inquiry, the observations of the parties and the opinions and suggestions expressed in the assembly in whatever form they were submitted;
(2)	To draw up proposals with a view to the settlement of the dispute brought before it under the council resolution dated February 19, 1932;
(3)	To submit these proposals to the assembly at the earliest possible moment.
On December 15, 1932, this special committee of nineteen drew up a resolution proposing that representatives of the governments of the United States of America and of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics should be invited to participate in the work of this committee, on the following terms;
In order to avoid misunderstanding and to make it plain that what is contemplated at the present stage with the cooperation of two countries not members of the league is solely the negotiation of a settlement by conciliation, the special committee suggests that it should be regarded for this purpose as a new committee, responsible for conducting negotiations, and

Sino-Japanese Dispute-Mr. Cahan
should be authorized in this capacity to invite the governments of the United States of America and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics to take part in its meetings.
This resolution contained the following closing paragraph:
In this connection the committee of nineteen considers that in the special circumstances which characterize the dispute a mere return to the conditions previous to September, 1931, would not suffice to insure a durable settlement and that the maintenance and recognition of the present regime in Manchuria could not be regarded as a solution.
On January 18, 1933, the government of Japan made an objection, stipulating that the committee to be1 appointed for the settlement of the dispute should include only members of the league.
The committee of nineteen further reported as follows:
On February 8 (1933) the Japanese representative submitted to the committee further amendments to the text prepared on December 15. On February 9 the committee, after considering these amendments, deemed it desirable to ask for further information in regard thereto, in particular whether the Japanese government accepted as one of the bases for the contemplated conciliation principle 7 in chapter IX of the report of the commission of inquiry regarding the establishment in Manchuria of a large measure of autonomy consisting with the sovereignty and administrative integrity of China. This question was submitted to the Japanese delegation in a letter of the same date.
The Japanese government replied on February 14 that it was convinced that the maintenance and recognition of the independence of Manehukuo were the only guarantee of peace in the far east and that the whole question would eventually be solved between Japan and China on that basis.
The committee of nineteen replied that the Japanese proposal of February 8 did not, in its opinion, form an acceptable basis for conciliation, and thereupon proceeded to draw up its report to the assembly.
In paragraph 4 of this report the committee of nineteen briefly reviewed the political and economic development of Manchuria during the preceding quarter of a century. This report says:
4	On the other hand, Japan had
acquired or claimed in Manchuria rights the effect of which was to restrict the exercise of sovereignty by China in a manner and to a degree quite exceptional. Japan governed the leased territory of Kwantung, exercising therein what amounted in practice to full sovereignty. Through the medium of the South Manchuria Railway, she administered the railway zones, including several towns and important parts of populous cities, such as Mukden and Changchun. In these areas, she had control of the police, taxes, education, and public utilities. She main-53719-320
tained armed forces in certain parts of the country: the army of Kwantung in the leased territory; railway guards in the railway zones; consular police in the various districts. Such a state of affairs might perhaps have continued without leading to complications and incessant disputes if it had been freely desired or accepted by both parties and if it had been the expression and manifestation of a well-understood policy of close economic and political cooperation. But, in the absence of such conditions, it was bound to lead to mutual misunderstandings and conflicts. The interconnection of respective rights, the uncertainty at times of the legal situation, the increasing opposition between the conception held by the Japanese of their special position in Manchuria, and the claims of Chinese nationalism were a further source of numerous incidents and disputes.
5.	Before September 18, 1931, each of the two parties had legitimate grievances against the other in Manchuria, Japan taking advantage of rights open to question and the Chinese authorities putting obstacles in the way of the exercise of rights which could not be contested. During the period immediately preceding the events of September 18th, various efforts were made to settle the questions outstanding between the two parties by the normal method of diplomatic negotiations and pacific means, and these means had not been exhausted. Nevertheless, the tension between Chinese and Japanese in Manchuria increased, and a movement of opinion in Japan advocated the settlement of all outstanding questions-if necessary, by force.
6. The present period of transition and national reconstruction in China, despite the efforts of the central government and the considerable progress already achieved, necessarily involves political disturbances, social disorder, and disruptive tendencies inseparable from a state of transition. It calls for the employment of a policy of international cooperation. One of the methods of that policy would be that the League of Nations would continue to afford China the technical assistance in modernizing her institutions which her government might request with a view to enabling the Chinese people to reorganize and consolidate the Chinese state.
The full application of the policy of international cooperation initiated at the Washington conference, the principles of which are still valid, has been delayed, chiefly by the violence of the anti-foreign propaganda carried on in China from time to time. In two respects- the use of the economic boycott and antiforeign teaching in schools-this propaganda has been pushed to such lengths that it has contributed to creating the atmosphere in which the present dispute broke out.
7.	The use of the boycott by the Chinese previous to the events of September 18, 1931, to express their indignation at certain incidents or to support certain claims could not fail to make a situation which was already tense still more tense.
The use of the boycott by China, subsequent to the events of September 18, 1931, falls under the category of reprisals.
The resolution of the assembly on February 24, 1933. also contains findings that the



Sino-Japanese Dispute-Mr. Cahan
sovereignty over Manchuria belongs to China, that the presence of Japanese troops outside the zone of the South Manchurian railway and their operations outside this zone are incompatible with the legal principles which should govern the settlement of the dispute, that these troops should be evacuated, and that the first object of further negotiations should be to organize this evacuation and to determine the methods, stages and time limits thereof.
The assembly also recommends the establishment in Manchuria, within a reasonable period, of an organization under the sovereignty of and compatible with the administrative integrity of China, which should provide a wide measure of autonomy, in harmony with local conditions, and which should take account of the multilateral treaties in force, the particular rights and interests of Japan, and the rights of third states; and that "the determination of the respective powers of and relations between the Chinese Central government and the local authorities should be made the subject of a declaration by the Chinese government having the force of an international undertaking." They also recommended that the Lytton report be followed by the organization of an international force which would preserve peace and good order in Manchuria as the Japanese troops should be retired. Briefly the position of Japan, taken not only before the assembly but at committee meetings and in private conversations, was that they had rights in Manchuria which were conceded by all the nations and even by the Chinese.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: May I ask what their rights were?

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext:
I am not going into that question, but. if my hon. friend will study the Lytton report he will find those rights enumerated in page after page, and to some of them I have referred. At least there is this much to their claim, that they won back Manchuria from Russia after China had failed to protect it and ceded it; under existing treaties they had the right to maintain railways through Manchuria; they had the right to maintain military forces there for the protection of those railways and the rights incidental thereto. They were in control, as the report said, of cities and towns; they had their own police, their own schools and their own educational system; and they occupied in Manchuria, by right of treaty, a position such as no other sovereign country enjoys in any other country in the world. And with regard to the profMr. Cahan.]
tection of these rights it was conceded by the Lytton report that they were entitled to give that protection, although the report found that they had exceeded their right in using their armed forces as they had done for that alleged end and purpose.
The issue that at once arose was this. Should the league assembly confine itself to making reasonable efforts towards effecting conciliation and the cooperation of these two countries, Japan and China, in Manchuria, under the nominal sovereignty of China? That was the supreme question we had in view at the time I delivered that address. There were representatives of other parties at the assembly who were insistent that the league should proceed to sanction more extreme (measures. Such measures had to be considered, but they might have meant ultimately involving Canada in a war in the far east for the protection of certain ill-defined interests, and it was certainly my duty, as a representative of Canada, to avoid saying or doing anything which would seem to imply that the government and the parliament of Canada were prepared to take such extreme action under the then existing circumstances. Further than that, the Lytton report suggested the formation of an international army of police for the maintenance of peace and good order in Manchuria, and the question at once arose as to who were to supply and maintain the troops, necessary to attain that end. Japan, through its representatives, daily in the corridors stated that it was prepared to withdraw its troops, but not for the purpose of admitting the bandit chieftains of China to come in and pillage and lay in waste tihat country again. That was their contention. But they took the view that if an international force could be organized and they could be relieved of the responsibility of maintaining peace in Manchuria they were quite willing to withdraw. I ask hon. members to put the question to themselves as it was put to me. How many thousands of troops, ten, twenty or twenty-five thousand, would Canada be prepared to put into the far east as part of a joint international force? I had to tell them in private, not in public, that I did not believe that under the then existing conditions the parliament of Canada would appropriate a single dollar toward maintaining a single company of troops in the far east for that purpose. And that was exactly the same position taken in private by the governments of England and France and by other governments of the chief European states. They were unwilling to sacrifice thousands of lives and to expend again millions of money for the sake

Sino-Japanese Dispute-Mr. Mackenzie King
of preserving, through an international organization of their military forces, continued peace in Manchuria.
I am not defending Japan. I think she went to the very extreme and committed acts that are indefensible, and I said so in that discussion. But I do say that I do not believe that any representative of tlhe government and parliament of Canada who has thoroughly studded the - situation can find very much to criticize in the statement which I then made. The hour is getting late, Mr. Chairman, and I have taken a much longer time than I anticipated, though I could in more detail have presented the case with regard to the maintenance of peace by an international armed force. I thank the committee for its courtesy.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext:
It is wholly
appropriate that the hon. the Secretary of State, if he and the government deemed it necessary and desirable, should make a statement to this house of the position taken by himself at the League of Nations in Geneva last year. I question very much however the propriety of that statement being made at this particular time and without any notice having been given the house in advance of the government's intention to introduce this subject at this session.
We have now reached what looks as if it might be the last day of the session and we are discussing the last but one of the items which appears in the final supplementary estimates. The question which my hon. friend has raised is of all controversial questions the largest in the world at the moment, and I submit that the government are not justified in having permitted this subject to be brought on without at least having given the house some advance notice of its intention to introduce it at this session.
I think it would be most unfortunate were the remarks made by the hon. the Secretary of State now to become the subject of comment and debate in this house. The parliament at Westminster has carefully avoided a discussion of the Sino-Japanese situation; the parliaments of most of the countries of Europe as well as the congress of the United States have done the same. I do not see that we in Canada would be acting wisely were we to depart from what has been, I think, a very wise restraint on the part of other deliberative assemblies, and to begin now a discussion of the Sino-Japanese situation. I prefer not either to approve or to disapprove of anything which the hon. the Secretary of State has said this morning, but to let his statement speak for itself as the statement which he made at Geneva did. The time may
53719-320J
come when the whole question can be discussed without danger of the remarks of anyone being interpreted by the nations that are at the moment in conflict as the taking of sides one way or the other with respect to the great questions which are at issue. It would be impossible, without going into the merits of the whole Sino-Japanese dispute, to comment on what my hon. friend has said and I do not think when these countries have been at war for the period they have, during all of which period we have kept out of the controversy, that we in Canada would be justified in choosing the dying moments of the session to raise a discussion on the questions at issue. I wish to be consistent with the view I have expressed by refraining from saying anything more at the moment. In my opinion this question might well have been made, if it was to be discussed at all, the subject of one of the most important debates of *the session; but seeing that it has not been discussed up to the present time I think that we might well reserve until a subsequent session, at which time we trust the Sino-Japanese war will have concluded, such further discussion as we may wish to have on the statement of the Secretary of State at Geneva and on his statement to parliament this morning. I have profound respect for my hon. friend's integrity and ability, as he knows, as well as for his years and for himself, but I question very much the soundness of his judgment in bringing up this question at all and more particularly at this time of the session.

remarks of the Secretary of State I wish to say pretty much what the leader of the opposition has said. I think the subject which the minister has brought before the house to-day is of very great importance not only to Canada but to the world, and if it was the intention of the government to have it discussed some notice should have been given the house in order that members who are interested in the international situation might have had an opportunity of preparing their material so as to discuss the subject as it ought to be discussed.
I could not always tell when the minister was quoting and when he was speaking for himself, but to me the whole trend of his discourse seemed to be towards the futility of the League of Nations, the futility of the signatories to all the peace pacts and the virtual declaration that the only hope of protection which any nation has, is in its own individual military powers. If, as the minister so emphatically declared, Canada is not

Sino-Japanese Dispute-Mr. Irvine
prepared to put one dollar or one man behind the League of Nations, then I do not think we ought to spend one dollar to send delegates over there to make speeches which we cannot back up and which we have no intention of backing up.
During the historical summary of the eastern situation by the minister I could not help noticing that great emphasis was placed upon the internal weakness of China and upon certain rights which Japan had to the occupation of Manchuria. In this case I think the League of Nations by its inaction has declared to the world as clearly as any declaration could be made in words that the whole idea of the league is impossible and that the institution is impotent. If it had been otherwise, surely the weakness of China to which the minister has referred should have been the chief cause for the League of Nations taking action. But it is stated that China is too weak for us to assist, that her internal troubles are too great and therefore we will let Japan go in with a disciplined force and do what she wants to do.
I am not going to argue this matter because I agree with the minister when he suggests that there should be no pronouncement of opinion on this affair without an adequate knowledge of all the facts. Under the cir-cmmstances it would be impossible for any member to become possessed of all the facts necessary to enable him to make a pronouncement. However, I do make this pronouncement:	either the League of Nations
means something or it means nothing. If it means anything at all, it should endeavour to make effective the steps provided for in its own articles. I venture to suggest that when the minister made the speech to which he referred he did not represent the general opinion of the people of Canada. They had at that time some faith in the League of Nations, they believed that Japan was invading China and that it was the duty of the League of Nations to stop that sort of invasion. Instead of doing that the League of Nations did nothing and left the whole situation to time and time was the very thing that Japan required. The invasion is continuing at the present moment. I suggest that there are only two possible courses for Canada to take. The League of Nations should be considered as an instrument of serious use and it should be used as a means of maintaining world peace; we should urge the enforcement of the provisions of the covenant against Japan and we should withdraw our official representatives from Japan
tltr. Irvine.]
as a protest against the invasion of China. We should either do that or throw up our hands as far as the League of Nations is concerned and have nothing more to do with it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
simply want to say that I agree entirely with the views of the leader of the opposition that it would be undesirable to discuss this far eastern question under present conditions. We would have certainly given notice if we had had an idea that there would be a debate upon the subject, but the government considered that the Secretaiy of State should make his statement so that it would be on record, not for discussion at the present time but for the information of hon. members.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: The only exception I take is to the subject being brought up at all at this time. I would .much rather have seen the statement of the Secretary of State appear in his autobiography which I hope he will give to the world some day and which I feel sure will be extremely valuable to those who have the privilege of reading it.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext:
I shall never publish an autobiography as I do not expect ever to have leisure sufficient to write one. But in my case, as with Japan, there was a great deal of provocation. Statements have been made on the public platforms in various parts of this country and in the press to the effect that there was only one side to the Sino-Japanese controversy. It was alleged that the position which I had taken had discredited Canada before the world. I trust I will not be considered egotistical when I say that my address before the assembly was listened to most intently. It was made after consultation with the other dominion members from time to time as they gathered together. The British delegation told me that they approved of what I had said, and some of the most eminent men in the assembly came to me afterwards to congratulate me upon having expressed the views I did, and others considered that it was the duty of Canada to call attention to certain facts because of our situation on the Pacific and our friendly relations with both China and Japan. I did not intend to provoke a controversy but I think it was due to me that I should be permitted to point out to this parliament the grounds underlying the expression of views which I made there. To-day is the first opportunity I have had of doing this.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of continuing this discussion but I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State. He stated that one of the reasons why Japan had certain rights in Manchuria was because China had ceded that province to Russia and that Japan had wrested it from Russia. I should like to know when the government of China ceded complete sovereignty Over the province of Manchuria to any country. I should like to know whether she did [DOT]that or just simply granted certain railway and trading rights.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Did I say "ceded"?

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Yes, you used the word "ceded".

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps that was not the correct word for me to use. As a matter of fact, China did acquiesce in the acquisition of Mandhuria by Russia.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Complete sovereignty?

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Russia took charge just the same as she is taking charge at the present time of northern Mongolia.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Did China consent?

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: She began to treat with respect to it. I do not know that Germany has ever consented to Alsace Lorraine being taken over by France but she has acquiesced. I am not emphasizing the position taken by Japan. But what I do say is this: Japan took Manchuria back from Russia. Japan then restored Manchuria to China in consideration of certain rights in and to Manchuria being retained by Japan, so that, so far as China is concerned, she has, one might use the word, ceded or granted to Japan certain rights which Japan now claims.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext:
My point is simply this:
When the word "ceded" is used, I thought the cession of a country meant handing over complete sovereignty, and I understood China had never done that to any other nation with regard to Manchuria.	.

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext: Was the statement made by the minister to the house this morning the official viewpoint of the government in regard to the dispute between China and Japan?

maintopic: SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTE-SPEECH OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE AT SPECIAL SESSION OF LEAGUE OF NATIONS
speechtext:
I am not pretending to make an official statement for the government with regard to the controversy between China and Japan; the time has not come for this government to make an official statement with regard to that, and the leader of the opposition has very properly taken that view. But
the time had come for the Secretary of State, who had represented Canada at the League of Nations and whose statements have been misrepresented throughout the length and breadth of this country, to show, by quotations from official documents that those who misrepresented those statements and who from time to time exaggerated them, have never thoroughly appreciated the purport of the report of the Lytton commission on which my statements were based.
Item agreed to.

Loan to the Chicoutimi harbour commissioners for the construction of harbour improvements and facilities, additional to the amount authorized by the Chicoutimi Harbour Loan Act, 1931, and to be subject to the provisions of the said act, $332,100.

Last night the Minister of Marine made a statement which I do not think he should have made. He left the impression that this item was inserted because of some verbal agreement that had been made by the former Liberal administration. I just want to make it quite clear that this item is for a-
Loan to the Chicoutimi harbour commissioners for the construction of harbour improvements and facilities, additional to the amount authorized by the Chicoutimi Harbour Loan Act, 1931, and to be subject to the provisions of the said act.
The present administration of which my hon. friend is a member, came into office in the summer of 1930. The Chicoutimi Harbour Loan Act was passed in 1931 and what is now being asked for is something in addition to the legislation which parliament enacted at that time. I do not think the minister should have even mentioned the former Liberal administration in connection with the item.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I was understood yesterday as
saying that this item was to cover works performed under verbal contract. That ivas not what I meant. I mentioned those facts only to show the difficulties we had to meet when the new commission took office.
I desire to explain this morning exactly the situation. The verbal agreement about which the contractor spoke to me when I was in Chicoutimi was in regard to an approach that he was building for the new bridge that the provincial authorities were supposed to build later on across the Saguenay river a few hundred feet above the pier in course of construction. The contractor contended then that.

Supply-Marine-Chicoutimi Harbour
he had a verbal promise from the former harbour commissioners that this approach was to be paid by them to the extent of $70,000. This morning I asked for information concerning the matter and I was told that the claim of the contractor was denied by the former commissioners and also denied by the present ones and was never paid. I am informed that the contractor is now endeavouring to obtain compensation from the provincial authorities. That is the situation in regard to the verbal contract about which he spoke to me, but it is over two years ago now and I spoke last night only from memory, so there is in this item nothing in connection with work done under a verbal agreement.

Do I understand the minister now to withdraw the statement he made last night which certainly would be understood as a reflection upon the previous administration and which he should not have made in the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have just given the exact information which, I think, is satisfactory to my right hon. friend; that is, that the claim of the contracts for $10,000 for work under supposed verbal agreement was denied by both commissions, past and present and never paid.
Then the statement the minister made last night is withdrawn,
That does not explain the item. Last night the minister gave us an explanation of the item. Now he says that that is not the explanation. Perhaps there is another one.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: This is to cover the amount due by the commission to the Bank of Montreal for money borrowed by the commissioners to liquidate outstanding liabilities. As a matter of fact, there were moneys overexpended before September, 1930, the date when the new commission came into office, *to complete the works which had been undertaken by the former administration, and additional commitments after that were necessary to complete the work. When the present commission took office, there was an amount outstanding at the bank and it was carried by the new commission. Later on they paid the bank, borrowing from another bank, and this is an oustanding liability, but it was to complete works undertaken under the contract entered into in 1927 by the former commission for the construction of that pier.
What was the amount outstanding owing to the bank under the old contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: At the present time?
No, at the time the new commission took office.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I cannot give the exact amount, but it was between $225,000 and $300,000.

Was there any authority
for the expenditure of that money by the old commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The contract was authorized, but the expenditure was over the estimate mentioned in the contract. There were certain works done by the former commission under the direction of the engineers to protect the works. A bulkhead was constructed and tie rods were fixed to solidify the works. That was done under the direction of the firm of A. D. Swan, the supervising engineers. Everything has been done under the direction of the engineers.

I understand that harbour commissions must come to the government and then to parliament for the necessary funds to make their improvements. From the statement which the minister has made, it appears that the former commission overspent the amount of money which was authorized by parliament for the improvements at Chicoutimi harbour. Is that not the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I can say that at the time the new commission came into office in September, 1930, there was a certain amount over-expended by the former commission.

I just take this opportunity of drawing to the attention of the committee the report made by Sir Alexander Gibb with regard to our different ports and harbours. Ever since I have been a member of the house, I have always supported any move which would make our ports more efficient in handling our imports and exports. When conditions were better than they are at the present time, Canada's trade yras growing very rapidly. In order to facilitate the exchange of our goods for the goods of other countries it was absolutely essential that we should have the best facilities that we could provide for the time being. I have even gone so far as to say that our facilities should be a little ahead of our requirements in view of our expanding trade. No doubt at the

Supply-Mmine-Chicoutimi Harbour
present time the facilities are more than ample, in view of the decline in the volume of business, to take care of our exports and imports.
I have watched the development of our harbours very closely since I have been a member of the house, and I am quite satisfied of this fact, that we need some central authority which will take into consideration our port requirements from a truly national aspect rather than considering them merely as local requirements. I am afraid that there has been too much local pressure brought to bear upon governments-I do not refer to any particular government-to provide facilities in ports which were not of any real value to the country. I am not, as I have already said, one of those who would skimp our ports of the facilities they should have, but I do think that between now and next session the government should take seriously into consideration the elimination of the harbour commissions that we now have and the placing of this work under one central authority who will look at the question in a national instead of merely in a local way.

In this item this amount is described as a loan to the Chicoutimi harbour commission. I would ask the minister why he is following that procedure? In the past the practice has always been to supply the money which is necessary for the harbour commissions, for port development, by means of legislation instead of through an estimate. In the past when a harbour commission required a certain amount of money for the development of a harbour, parliament was asked to vote the money through a special bill which provided for the payment of interest on the loan which was being made. But there is no provision here as to the interest which the Chicoutimi harbour commission may be called upon to pay to the government. Do I understand that the government will expect the Chicoutimi harbour commission to pay interest on this advance of money when it is in a position to do so, as harbour commissioners have always been bound to pay interest on moneys advanced to them by special legislation. This has always been the practice in the past. Why this change in procedure?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The demand was made a little late in the session, and we thought it would be shorter to bring down an estimate. I do not think it will make any difference, so far as the paying of interest is concerned, whether the loan is made through an estimate or by legislation.
There is no indication here at all that they are bound to pay interest on the loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: They are supposed to pay interest on all moneys loaned if they can afford to pay it.
But they are not supposed to pay interest that is not required of them, and there is no provision for the payment of interest in this item.
You cannot get blood out of a stone.

I know that many of these 'harbour developments were made at a time when business was better and prospects were brighter, and undoubtedly many of the developments in the different harbours could not be justified if you looked at them simply in regard to the volume of business to-day.

Such as the Montreal
harbour bridge.

My hon. friend is always
referring to that. Yet he has in his own department the Welland canal, which has never paid a cent to Canada, and which was supposed to cost, when the first estimate was brought before the house, $50,000,000.

How about the National
Transcontinental ?

Yet the Welland canal
which was first estimated to cost $50,000,000 has cost this country to-day $125,000,000, and nobody says a word, but my hon. friend is constantly referring to the Montreal harbour bridge. There are ten or fifteen undertakings under the government which have cost much more than the amount which was first estimated, yet my hon. friend objects every time to the bridge in the port of Montreal. Everybody was in favour of the building of that bridge. The Conservative party was as strong for it at that time as the Liberal party. Nobody on the opposition side had the courage at that time to stand up and say that they were opposed to the building of that bridge -nobody. During the last parliament when we brought forward the proposal for the building of the Caughnawaga bridge, the opposition of that day opposed the building of that bridge and any contribution from the federal government for that purpose, on the ground that it was going to be a toll bridge. The opposition of that time argued that the bridge should be a free bridge, and if we had proposed that it should be a free bridge the opposition of that day would have en-
5072	COMMONS
Supply-Marine-Chicoutimi Harbour
dorsed the -building of t'he Caughnawaga bridge. In the county of Chateauguay-Huntingdon the Conservatives went around saying, "The Liberals want to give you a toll bridge, but we are going to give you a free bridge." And now the Conservatives are denying the justification for the building of the Montreal bridge. It is true that we are not getting all the revenue at the present time that we expected from the Montreal bridge, but the revenues are increasing from year to year, and we hope that when the business of the country is once more reestablished we shall have very reasonable returns from that bridge, returns which will take care of all the expenditures. It is true that the bridge -has cost more than was originally estimated, but as I said, the Welland canal is in a much worse position in that respect than the Montreal bridge. There are many other undertakings of the government which have cost two or three times the amount estimated by the engineers, and that experience is not confined to government business alone. Any man who has had experience in construction knows that it is almost impossible to point to any work, even a construction costing only a few thousand dollars, that does not cost in the end more than was first esti-, mated by the engineers or architects.
The parliament buildings, for example.

That is a common experience because there are alwaj^s certain changes and new developments. The Montreal harbour bridge has cost a larger amount of money than was at first estimated because changes were made in the plans since the estimate was first presented to parliament. The steel, for instance, has been increased in strength and many changes were made in the concrete work. It can be very easily explained how the first estimate was seriously increased by these changes. The increase can be justified certainly just as well as my hon. friend can justify the increase in the cost of construction of the Welland canal over the first estimate.

I should like to point out that the opposition of that day did not oppose the Montreal harbour bridge because they thought it was going to be built at a reasonable price, instead of costing $19,000,000. The opposition of that day expected, and the government implied, that the bridge would cost eight or nine million dollars, but the government of that day that built the

bridge spent $19,000,000 on a property that should have been built for eight or nine million dollars. That is what happened in that case.
In regard to the Welland canal, my hon. friend's government while it was in power spent probably more money on the Welland canal than this government has spent. His government were in power from 1921 to 1930, and they carried on the building of the Welland canal. My hon. friend implied that it was our fault that the Welland canal cost a great deal more than the first estimate. My hon. friend can go back to his own party. He will perhaps remember the estimate that Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave of $13,000,000 for the building of the Transcontinental, a road which cost $178,000,000. My hon. friend, and this will come closer to home, can probably go back to the Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway purchase, which he forced upon the Canadian National Railways against the wishes of Sir Henry Thornton. Sir Henry Thornton said that it was not worth $5,000,000, and the hon. gentleman practically forced him to pay $6,000,000 for a road that has never yet paid its way in one day of its operation.

I am very glad indeed to
discuss the Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway. Since I -have been in -this house I have on many occasions noticed the expenditure of money for the building of railways which were mot as important as the Quebec, Montreal and Southern1 railway. This railway runs through one of the oldest sections of the province of Quebec, a section which has been established since the very first days of Canada, and that section of the province of Quebec has been the worst- served of all Canada so far as railway facilities are concerned. That section of Canada has been retarded in its development for twenty or thirty years, during which time its people have had to stand conditions so far as the lack of railway transportation is concerned that no other section in the whole of -this country could have sustained. I have voted, and hon. members opposite have voted, for the construction of branch lines where no people were established. We did that with a view to having people established there, or to having possession of a certain piece of territory in order to prevent one railway or another taking advantage of it. There were not many people established, but the purchase was for the purpose of future development. In the section in which the Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway was built there is a large farming population

Supply-Marine-Chicoutimi Harbour
and small industrial centres which for twenty-five or thirty years had been deprived of reasonable or fair railway communication. The small town of Sorel has been kept behind for a period of twenty-five or thirty years; it has not developed, along with other small towns, because of lack of necessary railway facilities. We had no regular train service. Freight rates were prohibitive, and it would cost more to transport merchandise from Montreal to Sorel than from Montreal to Quebec. That was the position in which we were placed at the time.
However no matter what was said by the Minister of Railways and Canals, the government need not be. afraid or ashamed because the Quebec, Montreal and Southern has been acquired. It is the best acquisition the Canadian National Railways ever made.
It has never paid its way.
It is a paying proposition.
It is not a paying proposition.

The minister cannot indicate a single branch line which has been acquired by the Canadian National Railways and is capable of giving a better showing than is the Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway. It was a good buy. It is not a load which has been placed upon the shoulders of the Canadian National. I am not afraid to put all the cards on the table, and when the cards are on the table I am ready to fight. I admit that certain officials of the Canadian National Railways were not strongly in favour of the acquisition of the line. They were not familiar with it. They did not know the circumstances under which that railroad had been operating, and they are always opposed to something new or something which had not originated in their minds. There is no man among all human beings who has a more one-track mind than has the railway man. He can see only one way. Everything coming from someone else he opposes or is ready to put aside.
Look at the returns of the Quebec, Montreal and Southern, and compare them with the returns obtained from other lines, and you will be forced to the conclusion, if you are reasonable and fair, that it was a good buy. It is the most promising line that the Canadian National Railways ever acquired. It was the intention of officials of the Canadian National to dispense with certain of their lines running from Montreal to Quebec and passing through St. Hyacinthe so that because of the absence
of grade, the lines of the Quebec, Montreal and Southern could be used. The road is level, because it is at the level of the St. Lawrence river. When business was good the Canadian National was contemplating moving all their freight traffic and even their best passenger trains along the Quebec, Montreal and Southern roads. That was the decision and proposal of officials of the Canadian National Railways. I repeat the line in question is not a burden, and even if it had been I humbly submit that the province of Quebec has less mileage per head of population than any other province in the dominion. The province of Quebec, which has not been used as well as other provinces in Canada, was entitled to something. It is unfair for the Minister of Railways and Canals to start an agitation on that point. Our claim was justified. The operation has justified the buying of the Quebec, Montreal and Southern.
Going back to the other argument concerning the Montreal bridge, offered by the Minister of Railways and Canals, may I say that-everything he has said is a justification for my argument. I refer the minister to an answer to a question asked in the house to the effect that the first estimate on the construction of the Montreal bridge was $12,000,000. That was the estimate of the engineers made at a time when the plans were not completed. Detailed plans had not been prepared, and to a large extent the minister could not do otherwise than resort to a certain amount of guessing when he was .asked to give the price for the building of the Montreal bridge. If the estimate made by the engineers was $12,000,000, there is nothing so extraordinary in the fact that the bridge cost $19,000,000, especially in view of the changes which were made in the material used, and in view of other circumstances including interest which was charged to the Montreal harbour commissioners on the cost of the land acquired for the bridge and the construction itself. In the $19,000,000 is included $2,000,000 interest. So, if we take everything into consideration there is nothing so extraordinary in the cost of the Montreal bridge. The discrepancy is far below that which existed between the estimated and the real cost of the Welland canal.

I have two minutes to speak before one o'clock. The hon. member stated repeatedly that the Quebec, Montreal and Southern was an advantage to the Canadian National Railways. The information I get from officials of the Canadian National is that the Quebec, Montreal and Southern
5074	COMMONS
Supply-Marine-Chicoutimi Harbour
has never paid its operating expenses,-and I believe my information is probably a little more correct than is that of the hon. member.
They tell you what you ask them.
No, they do not. If they told me only what I asked them they would be very poor officials.
When they do not tell you what you ask them, you get angry about it. That happened in committee.
Because one of the officials told a falsehood, I objected.
If he told a falsehood, fire him; that is the answer to that.

He told a falsehood in reply to one of the hon. member's questions; that is why he remembers it so well. The hon. member (Mr. Cardin) who just took his seat implied that I was objecting to the Quebec, Montreal and Southern and to the Montreal bridge because they were in the province of Quebec. I deny that, absolutely. There is no man in this house who is or always has been more friendly towards expenditures, or towards the friendly treatment of the province of Quebec, than I am, and I have been that way all my life. I think this is not a very broad attitude to take when, upon a matter touching the province of Quebec, the suggestion is made that we are attacking the French-Canadian population. I do not think that attitude is worthy of any hon. member on either side of the house. Hon. members on this side of the house definitely-
You are the only one who mentioned it.

The hon. member pointed out that because it was in Quebec I would have nothing to do with it. I submit that the statements which I made were correct, and had nothing to do with the portion of Canada in which the money was spent. I do not think it is fair to bring in a question of race in connection with a matter which we are discussing.

It was not brought in.
Progress reported.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO REMAINING LEGISLATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO REMAINING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the house was good enough to grant permission to revert to the orders of the day when we resumed at three o'clock, since I was inadvertently

that is a good word-detained by reason of the arrival of the United States minister.
This afternoon we propose to proceed with order No. 24, with the house in committee on Bill No. 99, if the item of business under consideration is disposed of. We propose to proceed also with Bill No. 100, which stands in my name, and with Bill No. 106. It was thought that possibly the difficulties to which attention has been directed in connection with the latter bill would be modified if not overcome by adding as a new paragraph a provision that this act shall come into force on a day to be fixed by the governor in council. That is the proposal we shall make with respect to that measure.
There still remains the redistribution bill, and I have asked the committee to report the bill to the house at the earliest possible moment. I am told that it might not be possible to report it until the morning, but I suppose that when it is reported it will take some time for consideration, though just how long I am not in a position to say. I regret that with respect to some of the provinces an agreement has not been reached, but that very often happens. I was on a committee twenty years ago, and the matter was finally disposed of only in the last two or three days. The present chairman of the select committee was on the redistribution committee ten years ago, and it will be recalled that the measure was not proceeded with as intended on the first occasion but was taken up at the following session.
Having regard to the fact that this is 1933, however, I think there is great anxiety on the part of the house that the bill should be enacted, and if we are unable to do so by consent I suppose the only other way is to invoke the aid of what is sometimes called the brute majority, but which constitutes the means by which under democratic institutions we carry on government, the history of which is very interesting but to refer to which would serve no good purpose. I believe an agreement has been arrived at with regard to most

Business of the House
of the provinces; I understand that the particular differences are very few but that unfortunately when an effort is made to overcome them new ones take their places. That being so it is quite obvious that the only proper thing is to report the bill to the house, and that will be done at the earliest possible moment.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING {Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, with reference to the remarks of the Prime Minister I might touch first on what he has proposed with respect to Bill No. 106, to amend the Canada Shipping Act. I understood the Prime Minister to say that he would propose that the measure should not come into force until so directed by the governor in council. I do not see that this alters in any particular the principle of the measure, which is one to which we at least on this side of the house cannot agree, and which we shall oppose on the second reading of the bill. I say that at once; the principle of the bill is not one which we can accept, and the proposed amendment would not help the situation at all.
With regard to the redistribution measure,
I cannot agree with the Prime Minister when he says that previous redistributions have not been effected by consent, that is, if we confine the statement to the last three redistribution acts. In 1892, I think it was, there was a redistribution which resulted in a long drawn out battle in the House of Commons. At that time Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who was leading the opposition, put forward the suggestion that there should be a joint committee of the house appointed to prepare the schedules to be attached to the bill to be presented to hon. members for their approval. In that year the government of the day itself prepared the bill without reference to the opposition, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier's view was that if a joint committee could be formed its members might be expected to rise above matters of party difference and do what would be generally recognized as fair and just to all concerned. After Sir Wilfrid came into office in 1896, and was confronted in 1902 with the first redistribution thereafter, he had redistribution carried out in that way. A joint committee was appointed from both sides of the house, and that committee arranged the constituencies as a result of agreement after some discussion and brought in a report which was unanimously accepted. To the bill was attached a schedule containing the redistribution map, and that bill was carried in the
commons without disagreement of any appreciable extent.
A few days ago I was speaking with Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden with regard to redistribution in his day. Sir Robert made it rather a boast to me at the time-and I think he quite rightly spoke with a degree of pride -that when he was in office which would be in 1912, a committee of the house had been appointed which joint committee came to an agreement, so that there was no controversy. With respect to the last redistribution, which was carried out in 1923 when the late Liberal government was in office, I recall the circumstances quite vividly because I had the responsibility in the matter that to-day rests with my right hon. friend. It did take the joint committee some little time to come to a final agreement but an agreement generally approved was reached. I believe that at the end there was one constituency with respect to which there remained some controversy. As I recall the circumstance it was not a matter that affected the boundaries of the constituency; it was I believe some other feature which at the moment I cannot recall.
I do remember, however, that the measure was brought into the house with the understanding on the part of the committee not that the particular difference whatever it was would be decided on the floor of the house but rather that the parties would declare their respective positions which I believe had reference to the returning officer to be appointed and that the bill should go through without any controversy, which it did. That was the last redistribution, and I have referred to the only other occasion on which we have had redistributions since we adopted the practice of having the redistribution map prepared by a joint committee of the house.
I do think it would be most unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, if at this time, after having been successful for the last thirty years with this method of effecting the necessary redistribution of constituencies, it should be found that the present ministry was not able to effect what three previous ministries effected in regard to a redistribution which would be regarded as fair and just by all parties concerned. I know there are some differences, but there may also be older and wiser heads in the house than those perhaps which have had thus far to do with the present redistribution, and I would submit that even yet, advantage might be taken of that added experience which in political life comes with years, to see if it is not possible to bring into this house before we prorogue a measure that

Business of the House
will commend itself with unanimity to hon. members and to the country. Having regard to the conditions which exist not only in our own country but throughout the world as well I cannot think of anything that would be more unfortunate than to have the popular belief in parliamentary institutions further shaken or undermined in any way. I would urge that very strongly upon the ministry as a reason why above all others, we at this time, should seek by our action 'here, irrespective of the parties to which we may belong, to let the general public see that with regard to the basis on which our whole 'Parliamentary institutions rests we are prepared to do the thing which will be regarded by the public at large, as fair, just and honourable. I believe the Prime Minister himself can bring his influence to bear in this matter. I cannot but think he wants to be fair, and he has a way of getting his own way when he wants it. I should say this was a time for him to exert that influence in the interests of fairness and justice.

My right hon. friend opposite knows from long experience-and he has had a longer fMr. Mackenzie King.]
experience of the responsibilities of the bead of a government than I have had-that there is a point always reached where you cannot expect men who belong to the majority to be told that they must subordinate entirely their views to the will of a sometimes arrogant and almost insolent minority. The committee is called for half past three this afternoon, and if there is a real disposition to overcome these difficulties it will then become apparent. If the older members of the 'house can assist in arriving at an amicable disposition of a highly contentious question, I shall be very glad; indeed, I shall ask the leader of the opposition whether he has any suggestion to make as to a member or two on his side who will cooperate with the older members on this side to enable such a. disposition to be arrived at.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO REMAINING LEGISLATION
speechtext: But I say at the threshold of the discussion that a frank recognition of the fact that there are Conservative members from Quebec and Saskatchewan is essential to the reaching of a conclusion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: That must be done; if it is not done, then the fault will rest not with the^ government but with those who assert their right to rule regardless of the rights of majorities.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO REMAINING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has referred to the provinces of Quebec and Saskatchewan as they were at the time of the last redistribution, and has said that the Conservative party was not represented on the committee that dealt with that redistribution. I submit that there could be no greater evidence of the fairness of the redistribution as effected in 1923 than the fact that to-day there are large numbers of representatives both from Saskatchewan and from Quebec sitting in the seats of hon. gentlemen opposite, whereas under the previous redistribution made when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, there was in one parliament at least, only one Conservative member, I think, from the province of Quebec and none from the province of Saskatchewan. The question is not whether there were representatives from these provinces on the committee at the time, but whether the representatives generally were able to effect a redistribution which was regarded by all as.

fair, and I submit that unless the members of the Conservative party on the redistribution committee representing other provinces had regarded the redistribution in that light, as regards both Saskatchewan and Quebec, the bill would not have received the unanimous consent it did.
I wish to take very strong exception to one phrase used by the Prime Minister. I believe that on reconsideration he will probably wish to withdraw it. He said if the matter were not settled by consent that no recourse would be left other than that of deciding the matter by brute majority.

-but we do
ask for the exercise of those qualities rather than brute force in the settlement of all questions which affect the rights of the people. After all, it is not merely our individual constituencies that are at stake but the representation of the people of Canada in their House of Commons. A more sacred duty does not exist than that which is imposed upon this house at the present time to see that that representation is made as fair and just as it can possibly be made, and if such is possible, that it be arrived at through agreement and fair play as the result of common consent.
I shall be very happy to join with the Prime Minister in naming two or three exministers of the crown from this side to meet with some of his colleagues, if he is agreeable to having that course adopted, and to allowing these gentlemen to see whether they cannot help to work out a joint agreement. I think it ought to be possible to attain such a result for I still believe that a desire for fair play and justice is what is uppermost in the minds of the majority here, irrespective of the parties to which they belong.

To provide for payment, as an honorarium, to His Honour Judge Edmund R. Wylie, for services as royal commissioner in connection with the Estevan mining dispute, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Judges Act, $1,000.

In connection with the Estevan strike, there is an incident to which I Should like to direct the attention of the governor,ont. It appears that a woman, a weaver by trade, living in England, was visiting relatives in the Estevan district that summer. On the day of the strike she went into Estevan to consult a doctor. While the rioting was in progress, she was sitting in the doctor's office. It appears that the policemen lost their heads and in firing, as they thought, over the heads of the strikers, they fired through the walls of the building in which the doctor's office was, one of the bullets striking this women in the arm. She was taken to the hospital where she remained for a considerable time. Her friends tried to get compensation for her from the provincial government, but they refused even so much as to pay her hospital bill, claiming that the mounted police were a federal body. Her friends wrote to me and I wrote to the Minister of Justice who replied that the federal authorities had no jurisdiction in the matter, because, although the mounted police were a federal body, they were at the time acting under the instructions of the provincial government. I ,do not think it is the intention of the people of Canada that their governments should resort to passing the buck in that manner. That is conduct befitting men like Messrs. Dodson and Fogg, but we expect something different from the federal government, and I would ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance whether he would not take the matter into consideration.
