speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am frank to say that the details of this matter have been presented to me for the first time in what has just been said by the hon. member for Weybum. But I believe there is involved in all these matters a principle that has to be settled, and I think members of the house as well as the public generally consider governments Should disregard principles because of the hardships of a particular -case. The old saying "Hard cases make bad law" is never better exemplified than when pressure is exerted upon a government to pay claims which are not valid, legal claims against it.
The question of the responsibility of the mounted police in a case of the character indicated by the hon. gentleman is not so easily disposed of as by a mere statement of the facts. The province of Saskatchewan pays to the federal government an annual sum, for Which this government supplies police force to that province. Saskatchewan has some executive responsibility with respect to the matter, and if the Minister of Justice has advised that at the moment in question the police force was acting under the direction of the provincial authorities, obviously the federal authority is not responsible. The question is one of fact. But I can only say this, that now that the matter has been brought to the attention of the government in the manner in which it has, I shall ask for the papers for the purpose of endeavouring to ascertain just whether any question of fact is at issue. But if one were to establish the precedent of responsibility, I can hardly see where the whole thing would end. I do not think I need remind the hon. gentleman that matters such as this are constantly arising and sometimes governments are charged with having hard hearts because they do not yield to pressure in any particular case. But if they did, then within a short time a hundred cases would arise of claims that would be asserted to be quite as substantial as the one that was acknowledged. This is one of the difficulties connected with the continuity of government and the maintenance of a proper relationship between responsibility and finance. If the financial responsibility is to be entirely disregarded, it follows that payments are made whenever a hard case is created. But if on the other hand a principle is to be adhered to, the payments are made very infrequently and usually in response to an appropriation submitted as an estimate to parliament or a judgment recovered in the exchequer court against the crown. Broadly, the rule has been, I think by most governments recently, especially having regard for 
the fact that in England it has been decided that the crown can be sued without its being necessary in certain instances to file a petition of right and receive the fiat of the sovereign, that permission to sue has been granted wherever there appears to be, shall I say, the semblance of a valid claim against the crown. I can only repeat that I will myself try to read the file and ascertain whether or not it is a case in which there is any responsibility, and if there is a doubtful case, without endeavouring to involve persons of little property in litigation, we may be able in some way to refer the matter to the decision of a judge for the purpose of having it disposed of. I cannot really state the case better perhaps than by directing attention to what has recently happened. The privy council this week gave judgment in connection with the old Yonge street corner in the city of Toronto. During a short interval when I was Minister of Justice I referred the matter to the exchequer court. Subsequently the judgment of the exchequer court and of the supreme court of Canada went to the privy council and the judgment of the supreme court of Canada was reversed by the privy council last week. There was involved a question of great principle which touched the relations of the crown with the subject. When the incurring of liability is at issue, the question of responsibility for negligence in connection with giving an order to fire is one that has engaged the attention of courts and of parliaments for a long time, the last concrete case heard in England being, as will be recalled, the case at Amritsar in India, where the order to fire was given, improperly it is claimed, resulting in a substantial number of people being killed. The hon. gentleman has anticipated what might be decided when he says that the police lost their heads, and that When the order to fire over the heads of the people was given they fired through the wall. If the wall shot through was higher than the people standing by, obviously the police fired over their heads but not high enough to escape going through the wall.

Item agreed to.
To provide for expenses of representation at the world economic conference, $15,000.

This item is to provide for representation at the world economic conference. I imagine if the Prime Minister is in a position to make a statement at the moment that the public would be interested in knowing something of the extent of Canada's representation at the world economic conference, and also something of

Supply-World Economic Conference
the personnel. I understand that there may be reasons why the Prime Minister cannot give full information but peihaps he will give uls as much as he can.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It will be observed that it is a very modest sum that is being appropriated for this purpose. It is a much lesser sum than was appropriated for the disarmament conference. My own personal views with respect to the world economic conference are that the position of ten millions of people on the northern half of this continent with respect to trade matters is of very considerable importance, and the voice of this country will have considerable influence by reason of the fact that our trading position is that of fifth or sixth among the nations of the world. It is therefore essential that we Should have such representation as will enable it to be clearly understood at the conference what our position is. But when you deal with what you might call the purely monetary and financial side of it I need hardly say to any member of this committee that the position of this dominion is not nearly so important because our relative wealth is not very great. That is best illustrated by the position to which I directed attention same time ago, that the half-yearly payment of gold made by Great Britain in December last really amounted to several million dollars more than the entire gold reserves of this country. The fact is that the representation of this country in my judgment will have to be determined in the light of the order in which the problems will be discussed, and I am not in a position to make any statement as to either the personnel or the extent to which this country will be represented because we are in much the same position as are other countries in that regard. The settlement of the order of business will have mudh to do with the representation that may be necessary.
My own personal view, I say to this committee frankly, is that I should be placed in a position where I could advise Ottawa as to what representation would be required to enable particular business to be dealt with. Once more I am giving my own personal view when I say that no good purpose is served by asking busy ministers to sit around London weeks at a time without being able to have their minds directed to the consideration of the problem with which they wish to deal. I dhall endeavour to ascertain the order of business and how it will be taken up, and then by communicating with those who I think are best able to deal with it I shall endeavour to see that adequate representation is afforded to this dominion.

On this item
I might 'as well ask the Prime Minister for information on one other point. The Prime Minister indicated that the government intended to appoint a royal commission to deal with monetary matters. I do not see any item in the estimates for the purposes of that commission. and I was wondering whether the matter had been overlooked or whether the government had in mind other means of making the necessary provision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I thank the right hon.
gentleman for directing attention to the matter. It was not thought that any sum that we might think reasonable to put in the estimates would be more than a guess at the moment. We propose to set up the commission, and there are means whereby we can provide for unforeseen contingencies of that character, as the right hon. gentleman knows, and as was done I think in. connection with the radio commission. That is in our mind, but it is just possible that the necessity for the payment of any substantial sum of money may not arise until after parliament will again be in session. That is the reason it is not in the estimates.
Will the Prime Minister say when the commission will be appointed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As a matter of fact our present view is that the commission Should consist of five members. That seems to be a rather large commission, but it is not so having regard to the necessity of obtaining the services of experienced men outside of this country, possibly to the number of two, together with three Canadians who might represent the practical operations of our banking act, the legislative position-shall I say? -of the country and-shall I say?-the great mass of the public who use credits and who are the customers of banks and are interested in the practical application of theories to the expansion of credits-that would be the third of the three Canadians. That is, practical banking experience; broad general knowledge of the operations of our credit system as relating to banking and currency and what is sometimes euphemistically referred to as the consumer; that is the user of credits and the applicant for credit. We feel that three Canadians should be appointed together with two whom we have not determined upon Who should live outside of this country in order that, if possible, a detached view might be obtained in matters of this kind.

The Prime
Minister has not answered the question I directed to him as to the time at which the commission would be appointed. In that connection, may I ask a question which I had intended to ask later, namely whether or not the Prime Minister contemplates the possibility of a fall session. I ask that question now because it relates in part to the possibility of having this commission sit in the interval, and alstf because hon. members would be glad to know at as early a date as possible if anything in the nature of a fall session is contemplated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have considered the
question with my colleagues. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
What is the
change made by the Senate?

The Senate did not concur
in the amendment contained in section 3, which deals with offences against morality and especially the corruption of children. Subsection 3 deals with an irrebuttable presumption; it was carried in this house and deleted in the Senate. I have reason to believe that at present pourparlers are going on with some senators, especially the leader of the Senate and Hon. Mr. Dandurand, as well as with some representatives of societies for the welfare of children, and that very likely some compromise will be arrived at and a new clause enacted which I hope will meet with the approval of this house.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE Mont-magny): I have had a certain amount of experience in criminal affairs, and I must say that in deleting this subsection I think the Senate showed more common sense than was shown by this house and conformed to the traditions of British justice as we understand it. Under the bill passed rather hurriedly in this house a man going into his own home while under the influence of liquor, even though it may be without the knowledge of his children, or permitting adultery even without the knowledge of his children, is liable to commitment on being found guilty of this offence. More than that, the onus is on the accused; he is not presumed to be innocent but must prove himself not guilty before the court.
I believe the bill should remain as it has been amended by the Senate; otherwise it will be an absolutely puritanical blue law. In my humble opinion, therefore, I think we should concur in the amendment made by the Senate and I would press the acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Dupre) to do so. I think we should remain faithful to the principle that an accused man is presumed to be innocent until he is proven guilty, and I do not think we should put on our statute book laws which are not capable of being applied or which, if they are applied, may lead to absolute tyranny.
Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker. Under this bill a man who is in his own house under the influence of liquor, if there are children, is presumed to be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to commitment whether or not they know of his condition, and he must prove himself innocent instead of the crown being compelled to prove him guilty. After my experience with criminal law, which unfortunately has extended over almost thirty years, I think this house should accept the amendment made by the Senate and thank that chamber for having made it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has misstated the case.
The Childrens Aid Societies of Canada have been endeavouring to prevent the corrupting of children's minds in their early days by reason of improper home surroundings. The new subsection 2 of subsection 215 read as follows:
Every person who, in the home of a child, participates in adultery, or in sexual immorality, or indulges in habitual drunkenness or any other form of vice, thereby endangering the morals of such child or rendering the home of such child an unfit place for such child to be in shall be guilty of an offence and liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year, or to both fine and imprisonment.
I need not say that this subsection in its entirety is not new; it existed before. The words added are, "Participates in adultery or indulges in habitual drunkenness." Drunkenness itself was an offence so far as that section was concerned, but the words now proposed are as I have just quoted. These provisions are intended to render it less easy for the child to have improper conceptions of things early in life. Subsection 3, which the Senate deletes, read:
It shall be an irrebuttable presumption, in any prosecution under subsection two of this section, that the child was in danger of being or becoming immoral, its morals injuriously affected and its home rendered an unfit place for it to be in, upon proof that the person accused did in fact, in the home of such child, participate in adultery, in sexual immorality, in habitual drunkenness, or in any other form of vice.
All that is new. Now, the irrebuttable presumption was not that of guilt at all. If the hon. gentleman had taken the trouble to read the subsection he would have observed that that is not what the irrebuttable presumption relates to. The irrebuttable presumption in any prosecution would be that the child was in danger of being or becoming immoral by reason of such surroundings as are described. That is, as the law stood previously, to prove drunkenness was not sufficient; it was necessary to prove something else. Now we say that it is an irrebuttable presumption under this subsection that the child was in danger of being or becoming immoral or of having its morals injuriously affected if the home conditions were as I have indicated. The Senate struck out that subsection. There is a medium course that has been suggested and I believe the Senate will probably accept it. The minister is therefore moving that the statute be sent back to the Senate for that purpose.

I may say that the Childrens Aid Societies of the country have been most active in connection with this matter, and this morning I received a telegram from a representative of the Childrens Aid Society, pointing out that if this subsection were deleted the legislation sought would be destroyed. While it may be puritanical to say that it is an irrebuttable presumption that the child is in danger of having its morals corrupted by reason of improper surroundings, that has nothing to do with the question of guilt or innocence. The guilt or innocence of the accused must be settled by proving in the first place, let us say, habitual drunkenness. That must be proven as a fact, but if you prove drunkenness there is an irrebuttable presumption that such a condition in the home is injurious to the morals of the child. I believe the Senate will now appreciate the fact that it was not an endeavour to determine the guilt and have innocence proven, but rather to determine the conditions that do exist; and having proven that there exist conditions which are detrimental to the interests of the child, that is a matter of irrebuttable presumption which is nothing more or less than what has been in the criminal code for centuries and will continue to be there. In other words, as a matter of law, certain inferences flow from the establishment of certain facts, and the proof of the facts rests with those who assert them, the onus probandi being on those who represent the prosecution; and when they prove the facts, then that is an irrebuttable presumption that the child is in surroundings which are inimical to its moral wellbeing.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I say to the committee at onoe that since we were last in session I have had the Civil Service Commission and Mr. Gladstone Murray endeavour to draft an amendment which would meet the situation in every detail, that is, to preserve the rights of the commission on the one hand and on the other to ensure efficiency. I am bound to say that I find to-day that they have not been able to arrive at any form of words which they consider adequate, so I propose,

Radio Broadcasting Act
with the consent of the committee, to add the following words in order to remove all possible doubts as to there being an infringement of the rights of the commission, in view of what was said the other day:
Provided that the contracts of service of such persons shall expire on the 31st day of March, 1934.
This is a temporary provision to ascertain how the act works out and it will only las>.t until 1934; on March 31, the end of this fiscal year, all persons employed under that section will have to be re-employed unless the law is amended under the civil service statute. They will have no position under this statute. What I said the other day has perhaps been extended a bit by some of our friends. When I said I proposed to set up the committee it was not to go over the whole radio question again-I regard that as settled-but rather for the purpose of ascertaining how the working of the statute which is now accepted as law could be improved upon in the light of the experience thus gained. This subsection, with the amendment I propose, would enable to be made only such appointments as will terminate on March 31, 1934, so that the creation of vested rights and interests, I humbly submit, could not arise.
In connection with appointments to the public service, my observation is that there should be a longer period of probation if possible, because I do not regard any system as infallible. It would be unfair to determine who were the best public servants, but I think a period of probation is very desirable, and all such persons, in the light of the experience that had been acquired, would be able to apply for positions and be dealt with in the manner thought best.
In section 14 I propose to add, in view of the criticism made the other evening, a few words which I think will be helpful. The new section 14 would read:
(1)	The commission may expend for the purposes of this act the moneys appropriated by parliament for such purposes, together with such sums of money as may _ be received by the commission from any business carried on by it under this act.	_
(2)	The moneys appropriated by parliament for such purposes shall not exceed the estimated revenue from receiving licences, private commercial broadcasting licences and amateur broadcasting licences:
Provided that if at the end of the fiscal year there is a balance of appropriated moneys unexpended, or if the revenue from the sources mentioned in this subsection exceeds the amount appropriated, parliament may appropriate any such balance and excess in addition to any appropriation provided hereunder.
(3) The commission shall present to the Minister of Finance an annual estimate of the expenditure proposed to be made by it during the fiscal year and the Minister of Finance shall from time to time pay into a chartered bank to the credit of the commission the moneys appropriated by parliament for the purposes of the commission.
From whait I have been able to ascertain I think it is (highly desirable that there should be a budget prepared by the commission to be submitted to the Minister of Finance in order that the payments made out of appropriations might bear a proper relation to the appropriations made by parliament and the moneys collected from: licence fees. I regard this as being purely a temporary effort to bridge existing difficulties in the operation of the commission. I was somewhat astonished at the exent of the condemnation of the commission to which I listened the other evening and I only hope that the committee will accept this as an effort temporarily to meet a situation between now and the end of the fiscal year. My present intention is to ask the same committee, providing the members are all living, which Bat before, to deal with this matter and investigate, not the principle because that was settled by the last report which was embodied in this legislation, but the operation of that legislation in the light of the facts as disclosed by the experience of the commission since it has been in office.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the first portion of my right hon. friend's remarks, that he purposes limiting this measure to March, 1934, I would point out that that does not meet our objection, an objection which I think is shared by the public at large, to having all officers, clerks and employees of the radio commission appointed by the commission itself and given such salaries as the commission itself may determine. So far as technical officers, professional employees, artists and the like are concerned, I think it is perfectly reasonable of the government to ask that the commission be given latitude and that they Should not be restricted in the selections which they make or possibly in the salaries and payments to these persons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

With regard to ordinary employees and clerks and the like, I cannot see any reason why those who come into the radio service should not be appointed in the same manner as those who come into the service of any other commission appointed by the government or even those who come into the public service generally. The Prime Minister has said that it is desirable to have a period of probation but he knows that there is a period of probation with civil service appointments.

speechtext: Six months.

Something like six months. During this period those who are not satisfactory may be rejected. I suggest that this section be amended by striking out the words "and other officers, clerks, and employees." The section would then read:
The commission may employ such technical and professional officers as the commission may deem necessary or desirable, and such persons shall receive such salaries or remuneration as may be fixed by the commission.
I think that would give the commission all the latitude it would need with respect to the classes that are at all likely to require special consideration. My right hon. friend knows that once a person is appointed to the public service he ought to have the right to assume that his appointment is going to remain permanent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is to remove that idea in this particular clause.

It will not remove it. My right hon. friend has stressed, and I do not think it can be stressed too strongly, the necessity of public confidence in this radio commission. In this connection I intend to speak very plainly. Here is a commission which has been appointed by a Conservative government, every individual member of the commission is a Conservative appointee. It is proposed to give to these Conservative appointees the right to make all other appointments under the commission, even down to the clerks, stenographers and the like. They are to be given the right not only to appoint but to determine the salaries to be paid. That will simply serve to create a great Conservative political machine. It cannot be called by any other name. I cannot see how it can be expected that public confidence tMr. Bennett.1
will be thereby established in the radio commission. If the government wished to take means to destroy confidence in this commission as an impartial body, they could not have gone about it in a more effective way. If the commissioners had been appointed as the result of a conference between the different parties of the house, or if there were on that commission representatives of the different parties, it might be a different matter, but hon. gentlemen opposite will not deny that all the commissioners are well known members of the Conservative party.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I deny that with respect to Colonel Steel.

One of them
was a former organizer of the party and I submit it is most unfair to give a body of that character the right to tnake all appointments and to control the whole radio broadr casting situation in Canada. I have seen some of the regulations already put out by the commission and they go the length of stating that the commission can suppress opinions on legislation passed by this parliament. What opportunity under such conditions is any party other than the Conservative party to have where radio broadcasting is concerned? It would be impossible to conceive of a more deliberate partisan act than that of giving to this commission the power to make all appointments. I ask the Prime Minister to consider the eliminating of these minor appointments from the control of the radio commission. He knows as well as I or any other hon. member that in ordinary administrative work there is nothing to distinguish what is to be performed under the radio broadcasting commission from that which is performed under any other commission. There is another reason why the Prime Minister, in particular, might well be disposed to give favourable consideration to this proposal. The Civil Service Commission as it is now and will be constituted is a body made up entirely of appointees of my right hon. friend and not appointees chosen jointly by both sides of the house.
Under the different measures which have been introduced by the government we are having set up in this country a number of what might be described as irresponsible bodies. They are not responsible to anybody. They are called commissions, board of trustees or something of the kind, and they are given all the powers that might be given to governments with respect to the particular field over which they operate. The Conservative government is to appoint trustees for the Canadian National Railways. These trustees

Radio Broadcasting Act
are to 'have to do with the expenditure of millions of dollars and the employment of hundreds of thousands of persons. They are to be given full control of the entire national railway service of the country. There is not a Liberal or a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation representative upon any of these bodies as they are constituted at the moment or as they are likely to be constituted. This radio broadcasting commission is being made into a sort of Conservative soviet and the same thing is happening with respect to the Civil Service Commission. What is government coming to in the country? Surely the minority is entitled to some consideration even at the hands of a majority such as that possessed by the government and its supporters. I think the government's action is most unfair and I believe it will be strongly resented by the people of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I have
only a few words to say as I do not want to delay the committee. However, I think it is my duty to support the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition. I think, by the amendments that are proposed in this bill, we are giving too wide powers to this commission. The commission has already been working for some time and I think I am expressing the opinion of many, if not the majority of the people of this country when I say that the commission has not lived up to what the people expected of it. I have no confidence in the commission and to give it the new powers that are intended to be given by this bill would make it impossible to secure the results we expected from the creation of a radio commission such as was proposed by the committee that investigated and reported on radio broadcasting. For that reason I am opposed to the bill and shall vote against it.

I have lived in Toronto for forty-five years. The leader of the Liberal party has stated that this is a partisan commission. May I say to him and to the committee that I have been associated with the Conservative party during all the time I have lived in Toronto; for the last good many years I have been in the inner circle and Mr. Charlesworth was never known as a Conservative in my city.	He was associated
with an old Liberal family and married into one. He was never in the inner circle of the Conservative party and not regarded as a Conservative. Of course he might have voted Conservative at some time or another. What is the use of casting it up
all the time that this is a commission composed of Conservatives, when it is not? As a matter of fact, I was not pleased with the appointment of Mr. Charlesworth because I thought a really good Tory should have been appointed.

Before this bill passes I want to say just a word with respect to clause one whidh amends the Radio Broadcasting Act and takes away from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission the matter of appointments. During the debates of Wednesday and Thursday of last week, when the Minister of Marine and the Prime Minister were speaking, they certainly gave to the house and the country the impression that the reason for this change was the recommendation of Mr. Gladstone Murray, director of broadcasting, brought over from England. Certainly the impression given to the house and the country by those hon. gentlemen was that this reputable director brought into Canada at the request of the government had stated that it was necessary to make this change, and therefore the government were falling in line in introducing this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I desire to correct my hon. friend in that respect. I stated very dearly to the house that since the commission had been in office, they noticed that they were handicapped in the performance of their duties by the existing law and this is why we are coming before the house with these amendments. They were approved by Major Gladstone Murray.

I am speaking with respect
to this one matter in particular. I have read my hon. friend's speech and I cannot find that he mentioned this particular item and it is specifically mentioned in the interim report of Mr. Gladstone Murray. As early as November, 1932, the chairman of the radio broadcasting commission wrote to the Civil Service Commission asking for the appointment of a director of publicity and a director of programs. I am not going to take the trouble to read the correspondence, but I Shall quote a sentence or two. The chairman states:
In connection wTith the organization of the work of the radio broadcasting commission, it is becoming urgently important that the services of a director of publicity be secured as well as a director of programs. I have discussed the matter with the Prime Minister, who assures me that the question is being taken up of an amendment to the act, whereby these and other important key positions on the staff of the commission may be exempted from the provisions of the Civil Service Act.

He then goes on to recommend that Mr. Buchanan and Mr. Weir be appointed at salaries of $6,500 per annum, and I shall have a word to say on that before I sit down. Nothing came of that and the next letter of interest is one of February 22, from the secretary of the Civil Service Commission to Mr. Charlesworth in reply to a letter of the latter again referring to the appointment of Mr. Buchanan. The secretary states in this letter that if they are going to make this a permanent position, they might just as well advertise now for a director of public relations rather than give him a temporary appointment of three months as they were able to do under section 40 of the Civil Service Act. He states quite frankly that the Civil Service Commission have no intention of certifying to such appointment, unless Mr. Charlesworth can give them assurance that the act is to be amended. This was all before Mr. Murray was ever in the country and certainly before he made any report to the government.
Then comes a very significant letter from Mr. Charlesworth to Mr. Foran, secretary of the Civil Service Commission, under date of February 23, 1933, as follows:
I have yours of February 22 relative to our request for the appointment of Mr. E. C. Buchanan as director of public relations.
I beg to advise you that last evening we received personal assurance from the Prime Minister that an amendment to the Radio Broadcasting Act would be submitted before the close of the session covering this as well as other matters. In accordance with the terms of your letter, I therefore ask that the certificate be issued for Mr. Buchanan as from February 15th.
That, I submit, proves conclusively that it was not Mr. Murray's recommendation that decided the course, but that the government had decided that they would amend the act long before Mr. Murray took any interest whatever in Canadian radio broadcasting.
May I say further that the danger of giving to this commission the power of making these appointments is pointed out fully in this correspondence in which they recommend that Mr. Buchanan-and I am not going into a discussion of his qualifications as a director of public relations-shall be appointed at a salary of $6,500. I am told that as regards directors of publicity in other departments, the salary of the highest paid official is around $4,000. Therefore this government, which under section 40 of the act is allowed, in making temporary appointments, to fix the salary, and which has been generous to its appointees in the way of salaries, did not feel that he was qualified to receive that salary and [Mr. Gray.J
they fixed one of $5,800 less 10 per cent. That, along with other dangers, is one of the reasons I am opposed to giving to this commission the power of making appointments of this kind.
Before I sit down, may I refer to just one other matter and that is that we now have printed by this commission 108 rules and regulations covering the broadcasting system, and I wish to direct the attention of the committee in particular to rule No. 9, as follows:
No broadcasting station may broadcast any speech, printed matter, program or advertising matter containing abusive or defamatory statements with regard to individuals or institutions or statements or suggestions contrary to the express purpose of any existing legislation; as for example, the Patent Medicine Act or any regulations promulgated thereunder.
I would like hon. members to take the rules and regulations as printed by the commission and read them one by one. If they do I think they will all agree with me that we are on our way, but where no one knows.

Will the minister give me some information with regard to section 14 of the act? collected by the Department of Marine from radio licences are deposited with the receiver general. Then when these moneys are released by a vote of the house the bills of the radio commission are paid, and that is controlled by the Finance department and the auditor general.

I would like to say a word
in support of the hon. member for West Lambton. I wish he had read a few paragraphs further on. It shows that the radio commission have taken power and have issued instructions that: no broadcast shall . . . issue statements or suggestions contrary to the express purpose of any existing legislation. Under that regulation it will be almost impossible for anyone to criticize over the radio at election time the actions of the government because that is legislation, but the government will be able to criticize the actions of the opposition because that is not legislation. The commission reserves the right to prohibit the broadcasting of any matter until the continuity or record or transcription or both have been submitted to the commission for examination and have been approved by them.
I presume that the commission sits in Montreal or Toronto, and if a man out in British Columbia suddenly has occasion or the urge during election time to express his sentiments over the radio he has to have them all written out-I do not suppose it could be done by wire because it would be too expensive-and he must submit them to the radio commission, and when they approve of his statement he will be allowed to go ahead and broadcast it. Then here is rule 93: The licensee shall file with the commission weekly in advance copy of the daily program schedule in such form as may be specified by the commission.
It is to be filed weekly in advance, by a man perhaps three thousand miles away. That rule could be used-I do not say that it will be, but the Scripture says, Avoid the appearance of evil-to discriminate against certain associations or bodies or individuals.

What is my hon. friend
quoting from?

From the rules and regulations of the Canadian radio broadcasting commission issued on April 15, 1933, P.C. 535. I agree with the hon. member for West Lamb-ton, who invited the members of the house to read these rules, because the more you read them the less you will think of them. On the face of it that seems all right, but if the radio commission and the Civil Service Commission cannot in a few days formulate a paragraph that would differentiate between those officials properly coming under the radio commission, such as professional and technical employees, and the ordinary employees who should come under the Civil Service Commission, they will not be able to do it at the end of nine months, and this will be the situation. At the end of nine months what chance will there be of turning these employees out? They will have a wife and eight children by that time and will be a pathetic proposition. Then there will be this further consideration. Unless they are absolute dubs, after nine months' experience of the work, which has to be learned for the first time, when they come before the Civil Service Commission for examination they will have to compete with men who know nothing whatever about the work and the Civil Service Commission will almost invariably give the positions to the men who have had experience. It is almost their duty to do so. One has had experience, and the other not.
In conclusion, I regret very much that I am not in the position of the hon. member for Weybum, to be able to boast, as he rightly does that he voted against the radio commission. I wish I had voted against it because the way it is developing it is going to be a curse to Canada, a curse to the people, and a curse to the government, a curse in the sense of being a source of perpetual annoyance and trouble. It will be another C.N.R. on a small scale. The minister told us some weeks ago that he was not sure whether he controlled the radio commission or the radio commission controlled him. There seems to be a doubt about it just as we hear the Minister of Railways say, "I cannot answer that question. I am not responsible. It is the railway commission." I regret very much that we adopted this system. Both sides of the house claim to be in favour of public ownership and then we
Radio Broadcasting Act

shirk our responsibilities and turn them over to a commission which has apparently far more power than the government and is responsible neither to God nor man so far as I can see. You will find that its expenses will increase. It will be such a ready source of increasing its revenue that the radio commission will say to the people, "The licence fee is now only two dollars. You surely would not begrudge three dollars now you are getting such beautiful programs." We have not heard the beautiful programs yet, but I agree that the commission must be given time to get into harness. There is, however, going to be perpetual trouble, and the licence fee will be increased, with more and more dissatisfaction on the part of the public. When the public are dissatisfied now they can, or they used to be able to, switch to another program. But now that this radio commission is in force they will sit down and write to the government or to their member expressing their dissatisfaction, and every mother will want the hour of the bedtime story changed to suit little Jimmie's convenience. They will make complaints that they never would make to a private corporation. It is bound to lead to endless trouble, and to judge from the personnel of the commission we are more than asking for trouble.

I agree with what has been said by my hon. friend from West Lamb ton and my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni. I have before me the rules and regulations of the Canadian radio broadcasting commission, National Research Building, Ottawa, April 1, 1933, and at page 17 in part V, dealing with the control of programs, I find that paragraph 90 reads:
No broadcasting station may broadcast any speech, printed matter, program or advertising matter containing abusive dr defamatory statements with regard to individuals or institutions-
With that I have no complaint:
-or statements or suggestions contrary to the express purpose of any existing legislation; as for example, the Patent Medicine Act or any regulations promulgated thereunder.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is competent for any one of us to criticize the Patent Medicine act or the Pure Poods act or the Hoof and Mouth Disease act or the Hay and Straw act or any other act, but if we do that, forsooth, Mr. Charleswortli will prevent the station from allowing us to broadcast. I think the slightest consideration on the part of members of this committee will lead them to the conclusion that whoever drafted these regula-
tions was not gifted with sufficient discretion to understand what he was doing. Take paragraph 91, for instance:
The commission reserves the right to prohibit the broadcasting of any matter until the continuity or record or transcription or both have been submitted to the commission for examination and have been approved by them.
Could there be any more strict censorship applied anywhere in the world? No one of my hon. friends opposite could make a speech in favour of the child welfare league, the social service league, the sons of temperance, the daughters of sin, or anything of that kind, without going to the radio broadcasting commission and asking Mr. Charlesworth kindly to peruse the full transcription of the language he was about to broadcast in support of any laudable movement. And here I believe they are infringing upon the ordinary laws of the land. Paragraph 95 is as follows:
Licensees broadcasting sustaining programs originating outside Canada shall, when requested by the commission, give priority to programs originating within Canada.
To that I have no very great objection. But listen to paragraph 96:
The licensees shall, upon the request of the commission, give right-of-way to such programs as in the judgment of the commission are of national interest.
And then:
In such event-
That is, where they give the right of way at the request of the commission.
-neither the licensee nor the commission shall incur any liability for compensation or damages.
That is to say, the licensee may have a contract with certain parties. Along comes the commission and states: "We think that such and such a broadcast is in the national interest; you have to abandon your contract." I ask hon. members of the legal persuasion if we are to confer upon this commission the right to give judgment concerning contracts. It seems to me that had the commission had a little more ordinary common sense they would not 'have drawn up such rules with regard to broadcasting. In that connection perhaps I shall have to differ from many hon. members on this side of the house by stating that I do not believe Mr. Thomas Maher, against whose appointment I have not a word to say- because he was a good politician and deserved recognition by his party

had anything to do with these regulations. He would have had too much political sense to have spread this sort of thing throughout the country. I do

Radio Broadcasting Act
suggest that perhaps it is the so-called nonpartisan member of the commission, a military man with the air of a martinet, who is endeavouring to dragoon the Canadian people into obedience to a commission which should never have been set up.
Mr. GAGiNON: I do not wMi to quarrel with the hon. member for Quebec South concerning hiis criticism of the regulations which have just been put into force. As a matter of fact they have not been in operation for more than fifteen days, and so far I 'have not read a single serious criticism of them.
You are hearing it now.

Those regulations will be in operation. As the Prime Minister has said, a special committee will be formed to study the operation of radio broadcasting in Canada, and at that time we will be in a better position to judge whether or not the regulations are in the public interest. May I quote an article which was published in the *Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph on April 6, of this year? As the hon. member for Quebec South must know, that newspaper is no longer a Conservative paper, but is Liberal.
I am not discussing that matter.

This article has been written with respect to the radio regulations:
Stand By Radio Regulation
An attempt is being made by American broadcasting interests to persuade the Canadian Radio commission to relax its five per cent advertising rule in connection with programs, by permitting an indefinite additional percentage of indirect or veiled publicity.
The commission should stand firmly by its rule and we believe that it has the necessary backbone to do so. The public doesn't want all the ballyhoo and vapid puffery that has been imposed upon it over the air in the past and would applaud if not merely ninety-five, but the whole ODe hundred per cent of each program were cultural or recreational.
But apart from this, an inefficient intrusion upon the newspaper's special field of revenue has forced the latter to discontinue its cooperation in the popularizing of radio as a great social asset.
Inveterate listeners-in sometimes complain because the newspaper does not publish programs for their convenience. But this is rather too much to expect when it is recalled that that program is a direct competitor of the newspaper's advertising columns and also includes, in not a few instances, information "pirated" from its news columns.	_
If and when, radio abandons its economic trespassing upon the newspaper, to which it owed so much in the days of its commercial infancy and to which it has made such poor
returns, publishers will doubtless be glad to supply their readers, who are also listeners-in, with day-by-day information as to programs, special features and so forth.
Meanwhile. Canada has rightly determined to keep commercialism under full control and we venture to predict that the day will yet come when the United States will be glad to follow the Canadian example, as it has done before now, in other instances.

I shall not insist because I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee, but it seems to me the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has taken a most amazing position. When I was reading a letter with respect to the broadcasting of a French program the hon. gentleman hastened to stop me, as though I were dealing with something contrary to the public interest. I have not been discussing
the question of whether the programs have been good, bad or indifferent; I have not
listened to them, so I do not know. I do object to the power placed in the hands of this commission, or to the power assumed by them. What right have these three appointees of hon. gentlemen opposite, however good they may be, to censor every word that may be said over the radio in Canada? What right have they to ask, under any circumstances, that if we wish to address the public we must supply them with a transcription of our remarks before we may speak?

That is not what the

I always bow to the opinion of the right hon. Prime Minister. Paragraph 91 states:
The commission reserves the right-

but they have not exercised it.

Surely the right hon. leader of the government is not trying to make a point there. I object to giving them the right to exercise that power, and the Prime Minister knows that is what I mean. I do not care whether or not they exercise it. I would not give the right hon. gentleman the right to do that if I had power to do so. Unfortunately he has sometimes tried to do it in the house, but there is such a thing as free speech in this country.

implication, on the part of the right hon. gentleman to the effect that I have not the right to speak as much as any other member of this house. If he has any reason for suggesting that I have not that right I challenge him now to state it.

I said, it depends on
what the hon. member is talking about, his personal observations. That was what I said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman drags into the debate personal observations and makes personal attacks, as he has often done, I say he is the last man that should do it-the very last man.

So that is the reason? My right hon. frignd objects to my protesting against censorship because forsooth on some occasions I have spoken in a manner displeasing to him. Well, that is one of the reasons perhaps that I do object to censorship. If every time I say something that does not please the right hon. gentleman or his friends I am to be prohibited from speaking, I have the right as a citizen of this country to protest, and I do protest and will continue to protest so long as regulations such as these are included among those issued by the commission.

When this bill was last
before the house I pointed out my objection to the amendment with respect to the removal from the Civil Service Commission of appointments to the radio broadcasting commission. By the radio broadcasting act of 1932, provision was made for appointments to the radio commission through the Civil Service Commission, but now it seems that instead of obtaining their staff through the Civil Service Commission the radio commission simply go to that body and say, "We want this particular individual with suoh and such qualifications," giving his name and designation and asking the Civil Service Commission to O.K. that particular appointment. That being refused by the Civil Service Commission, they went to the Prime Minister and suggested that he take away from the Civil Service Commission the power of making appointments. This is what I particularly object to, and certainly the amendment will not pass by my vote until that is remedied. All those employees that can be appointed by the Civil Service Commission should be selected by that commission rather than by the radio commission. I do admit

that there are certain persons, artists, who might properly be appointed by the radio commission, and such appointments should be left to them. Now the whole question of administration by the commission is under review, and the more we discuss it the more apparent it becomes that there is something radically wrong with the commission. In view of the rules and regulations that have been adopted I -think the whole question should be very seriously considered at the present time, and we Should determine just how far we will allow this tendency to go. It is just possible that the radio commission will be the first to put into effect the policy of the iron heel which we heard about last year, and we might as well have the fight now as at any other time.

One thing that has been discussed, something that is very serious, should be settled and that is the question whether the commission shall have the right of censorship or not. I am rather surprised that members of this house should suggest that any one, at any time or place, may say just what he pleases over the air. I do not think that such a thing is permitted anywhere; it is not permitted in the United States nor in Great Britain, and surely the House of Commons will not constitute itself a board of censors. The commission must have the right of censorship, and if after a given period their judgment should prove to have been at fault, then certainly parliament would have the right to ask for their dismissal. But, I repeat, they must be given the right of censorship, for I do not see how broadcasting could continue under a system whereby everyone could say over the air whatever he pleased, no matter how offensive. I have only this minute seen the regulations, but section 90 provides:
No broadcasting station may broadcast any speech, printed matter, program or advertising matter containing abusive or defamatory statements with regard to individuals or institutions,-
That is right.
Well, how will you stop that without censorship?
Read the rest.
[DOT]-or statements or suggestions contrary to the express purpose of any existing legislation; . . .

I wonder whether my hon. friends have listened during the last two and a half or three years to the patent medicine

quackery put over the radio in contravention of the Patent Medicine Act. I would point out that similar regulations appear in every broadcasting act I have read, and they are necessary if radio broadcasting is to be properly carried on.

My hon. friend refers to people saying over the radio things they are prohibited by law from saying. I say, make any prohibitions you like, but make them by law and have them enforced. But that is not what that says; that is what it may mean but it is not what it says. Under that section the commission has power to control the political utterances of members of this house. Does my

Why, it is an outrage. Surely this is a country of free speech, and if we are to have radio broadcasting then every one of us has the right to express his opinions over the air no matter how disagreeable those opinions may be to the rest of us. The Minister of Marine took me to task by Saying that I was objecting to free speech. The speeches to which I re-

ferred embodied criticisms of the administration of the city of Montreal and t'he provincial government. 1 should like to know if these regulations were in force when those speeches were delivered.
