use that may be made of radio stations, I submit that the Minister of Marine or the Prime Minister should make a declaration to the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these
regulations were submitted by the commission to the council and sent by the council to the Minister of Justice. The Department of Justice made certain amendments to them and sent them back as being in order. The power given to the commission is stated in the act. I was amazed at the attitude taken by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay because there is nothing in these regulations that I know of to compel a member to submit his speech to the commission before it is made. What is stated is that the right is reserved to require submission if occasion necessitates. The reservation of that right is copied largely from the English rules. It is a supervision to -be exercised in times of great stress and to deal with provocative discussions over the radio to which many people do not like to listen. All I have to say about this matter can be said in a few sentences.
Does this committee mean to indicate that it desires to destroy this commission? Is there any way in which this business of broadcasting can be carried on except through a department of government or through a commission? If it is to be carried on through a department of government, then the whole condition would change with a change in administration. It would be a political machine from the start. If it is not to be carried on through a department of government, what instrumentality shall be used for the purpose? The answer of this committee and of this statute is-a commission. Therefore, we have negatived the idea that this broadcasting business is to be carried on as a department of government and we have concluded affirmatively that it shall be carried on by a commission as an instrumentality of government. I think the committee must agree to these two propositions. Having concluded that we will set up a commission as an instrumentality of government, we must then proceed to the appointment of the commission. There has been much criticism of the appointments which were made. I confess that I know very little of the chairman's politics. I did not know him personally except for having met him two or three times at public functions. He was highly spoken of by independent persons to whom I went for assistance in this very difficult task of selecting a chairman. It was believed that his wide knowledge of Canada and his experience as a dramatic critic

Radio Broadcasting Act
would entitle him to have some idea of the tastes of Canadian people in broadcast programs and that in the preparation of programs he would have better ability than the average man would have in connection with matters of that kind. At any rate, he was selected as chairman and his appointment was hailed with much acclaim by the press of all classes of political thought. The truth is that I was surprised the other evening to hear the statement made as to his unfitness for the position.
I believed when he was appointed he had singular qualifications for that particular post and that he would be able to understand something of the Canadian viewpoint, of Canadian history. The books he has written indicate a strong, virile Canadian sentiment and I believed, as I have said, he would be able to appreciate what the Canadian people would wish to have.
The leader of the opposition speaks of three political appointees of this government.
I know nothing of the qualifications of the technical officer and I have never inquired.
I know he was highly spoken of m his profession; I believe he was awarded the Military Cross during the war, and though the information is always open to question, technical persons to whom I have applie for it have told me that Colonel Steel occupies a unique position with respect to matters of broadcasting and knowledge of the technique of electricity. I know from a source that has thus far been accurate, that on many occasions he has been offered outside this country positions in connection with the industrial field of the development of radio that would give him much greater compensation than he is now receiving, but he has a very earnest desire to continue along the line he has been pursuing in Canada in connection with the development of electrical appliances and especially in connection with radio broadcasting. I think it is rather unfair to say that in any sense he is a political appointee. He has, so far as I know, never indicated anything of his political beliefs and faith, and I certainly never have had any talks with him about his political views. He is perhaps given to expressing his opinions very tersely; perhaps, in the language of a distinguished man of another age, he does not suffer fools gladly, but that may be a misfortune. At any rate I am bound to say that very great harm is being done by suggesting that this is in any sense a political appointment.
So far as Mr. Maher is concerned I am not going over this afternoon what I stated the other day.
A commission having been appointed to which some hon. gentlemen take exception, the next thing to do is to assist it to discharge its functions. If anyone thinks you can appoint a commission to handle national broadcasting in Canada without tramping on the toes of private interests in this country, he is mistaken. Those who own private stations and those who think they should have control of the industry or business in Canada are all opposed to this commission and its pathway is made increasingly difficult by reason of that fact. Wave lengths have not in the past been treated with just that high regard to international obligations that will have to be observed in the days to come, because as we go forward in this matter, there is a more strict supervision and the international phase of the situation calls for much more careful consideration. I do not desire to repeat this, but the international side of the matter is the one that causes the acute difficulty. On the other side of the line we have 120,000,000 people with the most powerful stations except one in the world and unfortunately the impulse behind the human voice when it goes out into space to vibrate is one that may send it north or south or east or west.
Fortunately.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman prefers the voices from most other countries to those of his own, but I ask him in this instance to believe me when I say that I do not think it is at all times fortunate that the voices of other countries should drown the voices from this. I mention that merely because it is that difficulty with which those gentlemen have to deal. That is purely the technical side of the matter.
There is also another side to it, that is, the question of the preparation of programs. I think the programs that have been offered to the Canadian people, in view of the fact that this is a new commission, have not been unworthy of some of our traditions. I have not been able to listen in on the radio during the last few months except, I think, on a Sunday, and I remember hearing a very admirable lecture. I was pleased to leam at the end of it, as it touched the early history of the country, it was under the auspices of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission. We have in Canada a history that lends itself to broadcasting; we have the history of the early pioneers going back four hundred years to the early settlers, the history of the government of this country, of our

Radio Broadcasting Act

commercial expansion and our growth and development constitutionally and otherwise. All these are subjects that might well foe treated by the commission and I believe they will be, but it can function only if it is not destroyed, as I said the other evening, by its friends. It has to make regulations. The making of regulations, one would think, to listen to some of the observations made here this afternoon, is a terrible thing. But every hon. member knows he cannot send a telegram using profanity or obscenity.

There is no censorship
there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The statute states that if anyone writes such a telegram, the telegraph company will not transmit it. You cannot write any telegram you like and have it sent. So you cannot print any kind of advertisement you might like, because the newspaper will not publish anything the publication of which is not permitted by law. In addition to that you have the censorship that arises by reason of the fact that this is not the printed but the spoken word, and if the spoken word is to be sent on the air regardless of what it may be, you will have an intolerable condition in this country. Children, all kinds of people, would not desire to hear either profanity or sedition or obscenity over the radio. The right of censorship has been exercised by every radio commission I know anything about. The word "censorship" sounds offensive to the average mind because it means the paramount authority of the state is not willing there should be absolute licence on the part of each individual citizen. There can be no civilization without curtailment of individual rights and in this instance the freedom of the individual is limited by the exercise of censorship, if you call it such, by a commission. The commission drew up these regulations which, as I have said, were sent to the Department of Justice and reported back, after some amendments had been made, as being in proper form; those are the regulations to which reference has been made. The fact that prohibitory power is expressed does not of course indicate it is at all times to be used. To reserve the right to do something means that you have not departed from that right. Upon that you cannot build an argument that a speech must be examined before it is made. It is really an indication that the right is still reserved and has not been parted with to exercise the censoring power.
But I go further. There is not one of us who has not every day to make some sacrifice of his individual freedom. The by-laws of 
the city of Ottawa, the provisions of the statutes of the provinces and of the dominion, control individual liberty with respect to various matters. A statute which we had before us torday dealt with the question of habitual drunkenness in a home being an offence against good morals so far as children are concerned. In this case we have a censorship set up, not merely to exercise censorship, but to protect and ensure the success of this enterprise of ours. I use the word "ours". I do not think it is deliberate; I am sure it is not, but the attitude taken in this committee by hon. gentlemen opposite has given great succor and support to those who desire to destroy publicly-owned broadcasting in Canada, and who have taken to themselves the thought that this country regrets that it has nationalized radio. These interests have taken new force and new life because they say that this house which a year ago spoke with unanimity is now bitterly engaged in a discussion the like of which we have hardly had this session, in the character of the language used and the expressions applied to individuals who are outside the pale of the house but who are nevertheless subject to criticism. And criticism too of men who came here at the courteous request of the government to give us the benefit of their experience of the most extensive broadcasting system in the world, that of the British, because although the soviet have more powerful stations than England the British is the most important broadcasting system.
In the course of experience it was found that you could not go to the Civil Service Commission and get the kind of persons required for particular positions on an advertising basis, on a tender basis, so to speak, and the radio commission sought amendments to the statute. The amendments they first sought were far more comprehensive than the ones now before the house, and personally I said that they were too extensive and that I did not care to ask parliament to grant them. I was not so much impressed in the first instance with the necessity of the amendments with respect to the Civil Service Commission until after Mr. Murray had given us the benefit of his views.
I do not pretend that Mr. Murray's views are binding upon me in any sense, but he was a Canadian who had much experience and had made for himself a position for his services in connection with which he is being paid, a salary that to some hon. members of this house would seem to be princely; he was of the opinion from his experience that at least in the initial stages of our work, if we are to get the radio commission functioning properly, because we have to appoint provincial representatives,

Radio Broadcasting Act
and advisory committees must be set up in order to assist in carrying out in each of the nine provinces the work of the commission, it was desirable that the commission should be able to employ those servants and employees who could best do the work. I said to the radio commission, and I say to this committee frankly: It is contrary to the spirit of the Civil Service Act. But it was urged upon me that we could not deal with the matter in that way.
Once more reference has been made to the Civil Service Commission as being an organization that reflects the mind of the government. As I said to this committee the other day, we promoted to membership in that commission one of the members of the civil service, and I do not know to-day what his political faith is. I haven't any idea what Mr. Bland's politics are. In fact, I asked one of my secretaries the other day if he knew, and he said he did not, but he said he believed that if he had any views one way or the other they were probably Liberal. That was the answer given to me. But I personally know nothing of Mr. Bland's politics. I recommended that he should be promoted to the position he now holds because I believed that it was the view of the committee of this house that sat last year that he was an exceptionally well qualified man. Certainly in this house it was so stated. All that I know about him is this: Before he was appointed I sent for him and I asked him if he had any recommendations to make about the situation generally. He told me he thought money could be saved. I asked him if he was willing to accept the position on that commission and give it the benefit of his wide experience, amd he said he was, and he was promoted accordingly. That is the political side of that appointment. Doctor Roche is still there.
What about the third member?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He has not yet been appointed.
Does not the Prime Minister think it is important that he should be appointed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is important that any vacancy should be filled if there is necessity for it, but there is no crying demand for it and the position is not yet filled because of an earnest endeavour to seek one who may not be charged with being a mere partisan. Doctor Roche and Mr. Bland are the first to realize that they cannot fill all these positions satisfactorily under the existing provisions of the Civil Service Act; but they believe that 53719-322^
the provisions of the act are wide enough to exempt these positions from its operations. As the law now stands it reads:
The commission may employ such technical, professional and other officers, and clerks and employees as may be necessary. Such officers, clerks and employees shall be appointed pursuant to the Civil Service Act.
That is the law as it is to-day. That is found to be unsatisfactory, unequal to the demands made upon it.
I have only one idea about this broadcasting commission, and that is to see it succeed. I know hon. gentlemen think that everyone is thinking in terms of political considerations. With respect to this matter I have not a thought in the world about politics, and I have not had. I explained the other evening the circumstances in connection with the appointment of one member of the radio commission, and I have also indicated this afternoon the position in respect to the other two members. We say that the proper method to pursue to meet the situation is to amend the statute so as to allow the radio commission to. make these appointments. I am quite willing to admit that the criticism of that proposal is a criticism that I would make if I were sitting opposite, that the appointments were being put solely in the hands of the radio commission as well as the payment of salaries and matters of that kind, and yet when the advisory tariff board came into being under the late administration, a gentleman was selected for chairman who while he was on the commission was nominated as a candidate of the party in power, and there was no question about that at all, and who had previously been a candidate and been defeated. I am not going to say that human nature in any sense is at all different on one side of the house from the other. We are more or less the same. But the government thinks, in view of the representations made and the experience which the commission has had, it should be enabled to employ such persons as it finds necessary to carry on its business. It is because I and my colleagues in the government desire to protect the Civil Service Act and the principles of it that I suggested this afternoon, after thinking it over, and after these gentlemen had discussed it among themselves, no term of engagement should extend longer than the thirty-first of March next, that they would all expire on that date, so that there will be no question about an opportunity being afforded to make a discriminating effort to determine those persons who should be appointed under the Civil Service Act as distinguished from those to be employed by the radio commission itself.
Radio Broadcasting Act

The leader of the opposition has suggested that we strike out all the words after "officers," leaving in only the technical and professional officers. But it is with respect to the other officers, the director of programs, the director of public relations, if you will, and other such positions, that the commission in. England at least, found that they had to have the freest hand in order to deal with the situation as it might arise. But in order that no one might be prejudiced I suggest this limitation of time.
My hon. friends opposite say, "This means that those people who will be employed in the meantime will have a better chance to get the position than someone else." But they would get it then under the provisions of the statute, being the best able, and if they are the best, those are the ones we want in order that the commission may succeed. I say frankly to this committee that it is my profound conviction, so far as a man can dissociate himself from political beliefs in a matter of this kind, that unless we endeavour to make a united effort to save this business as a national asset we are going to see it fail, and if it fails you may say that that will be a reflection on the government, and that is what you want to see happen. But it goes deeper than that. It is a reflection upon the people themselves, on their ability to maintain a public enterprise as a public property. That is what it really is, and that is the reason I make this suggestion. But if there is any other suggestion that this committee can make more adequately to meet this situation, and that will permit this commission to lay the foundations of the structure upon which it hopes to build success, by employing suitable instruments to that end; if there is any suggestion to make other than the one I have made concerning the limitation as to time of appointment, I shall be glad indeed to consider it and if possible to accept it. Because one thing is sure, namely, that the instrumentality we have set up to accomplish our end, namely, the commission-and after all it is the instrumentality of the government-can function only if we give it a chance to function.
I am sorry to say that in view of the protracted discussion over this matter it will be thought abroad, as it is already thought, that we rue our bargain with respect to the radio commission, that we are no longer desirous of [DOT] maintaining it as a public asset, and that we are convinced that we should hand radio over to private interests. Well, just imagine what private interests have done in connection with other enterprises in this country.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And just imagine what they would be doing now if they had this in their hands. They would have no restrictions upon whom they would employ, no limitations imposed upon them. They would go forward with licence fees, if we gave them the licence fees, and do their task in that way. We do not get up in this House of Commons and ask, concerning the railway commission: "What induced them to close the crossing on Broad street, Regina?" or, "What was the operating cost concerning the grade separation on Yonge street?" or, "Why did they do thus and so?" We appoint them, and we leave them to do their work and perform their duties. Every time they have requisitioned us for additional assistance, whether it be for engineering-and they have increased those payments frequently-or whether it be for economies here or there, we have yielded to their views, because it is an instrumentality of government which the government itself could not operate as a department of government. The difference between departmental government and government by commission as an instrumentality of government is so clear that it need not again be defined.
We have taken other commissions-the grain commission, for instance. Look at what the grain commission is doing. It is operating through its laboratory in Winnipeg, through its agencies in Fort William, Calgary, Edmonton and Moose Jaw, and is discharging its multifarious duties. Is anybody in this house saying: "Look at the terrible regulations they have passed."
They did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And properly so, too.
Every weighing master was under criticism.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And properly so, too.
No, not properly so, because the committee did not find it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
realizes that the regulation was beyond the powers of those who enacted it. That is the point. That did happen, and it does happen frequently, and when power is exceeded you have the inevitable criticism and you have an adjustment of the difficulties. But the grain commission is operating all through western Canada-elevators, grading, standards, and everything pertaining to grain. And the value of the grain commission's work to-day lies in the value of its standards and grades abroad, and the confidence the public have in their integrity and the manner in which they discharge their duties. With perhaps

Genter Thickener Company
some minor exceptions there have been few criticisms with respect to appointments made to the grain commission. It is true I could name one or two cases where there have been criticisms. One unfortunate gentleman was never able to sit at all-he was dying when he was appointed. But that is not a matter of importance. Let us take the railway commission: True, it has been the harbour of refuge once or twice, and still is. It is true that political considerations affected judgments now and then, but in the main we have set up an instrument which has succeeded.
I go farther: You have the harbour commissions. There you have had great failures and some successes. But so long as you have public -opinion responsive to earnest effort you have an opportunity to achieve success. But if in a spirit of carping criticism, without referring to any other fact, you have concluded that what we have to do is to find fault with a body that has not yet launched upon its work-I claim a fair attitude is not being adopted. I carry my mind back to what took place in connection with the old grain commission, and how difficult it was to get it started. I wonder if this committee realizes how great the task was and how violent the criticism was, not in this house but-
It made a good commission eventually, though, and made good regulations eventually.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say that the commission as a commission, whose findings with respect to grades and matters of that kind have been received throughout the world with confidence, as I said a minute ago has in the main discharged its duties well. I could give striking illustrations, if I so desired, in respect of every one of them in which I believe political considerations governed1 appointments; I could give illustrations one after the other. But there is no necessity of doing that, because we all know that in the main with respect to these matters the Canadian people are satisfied.
This question of radio is more important than all of them.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it is more important, because it touches the lives of all. The others touch the lives of some, but this is universal; it diffuses and dispenses news which comes into the homes of the poorest-because we find many poor homes in this country in which there are. small radio sets, notwithstanding the fact that they find difficulty in obtaining other things which are almost necessities. They have a desire to hear what is going on in the outside world. While grain might be sold because of its superior quality even if the grades had never been fixed or determined upon-as they were not before, and as they are not in Russia, a country selling her grain in competition with ours-and while railways might be dealt with as they were before there was a railway commission, yet here we have something which shapes, forms and moulds the character of our Canadian people. And to the extent to which a commission realizes its responsibilities, and is able to discharge the functions which by this legislation devolve upon it, it will have discharged its duties as you and I would like to have them discharged. iSo to shape and mould the whole national outlook of the Canadian people as to make them take an interest and pride in the development of their own organization, in my judgment is at least a consideration. But I am not unmindful of the fact that keeping up with the Joneses has been one of the great difficulties of the present day. And to-day one of the difficulties that we Canadians have to face arises from the fact that we have limited resources and that we think we should have something just as good as if they were unlimited.'
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. E. R. E. CHEVRIER (Ottawa) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 102, respecting a certain patent of Genter Thickener Company.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Extension of time for application to revive patent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The other evening I asked that this bill stand because I hoped the minister would be able to look into it. I was unable to investigate it myself but I had that done, and the report I received was that because of a mistake made by a firm of solicitors in New York-an entry had been made in a diary to take the proper action to extend the patent, but that was not done-
Radio Broadcasting Act

the solicitors were framing this measure in order to protect their client against their own negligence. I do not know whether that is a correct statement but that is the report I received. In view of the closing sentences of the section, in which the matter is left in the hands of the commissioner of patents after they have established the facts, I know of no reason why the matter should not be left in that position.

May I say that the right hon. gentleman is quite right in his understanding of the facts. There was a motion for the return of the fees, and I wonder if there is any chance of that being done. I do not want that motion prejudiced by reason of my not mentioning it at this time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Minister of Finance is not in his place, but I see no reason why the fees should be returned. I distinctly recall that once in the practice of my profession a mistake was made in my office and I had to pay $1,000 to rectify it. I see no reason why this country should make the contribution instead of the solicitors.

Section agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed. RADIO BROADCASTING ACT

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 99, to amend the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, 1932-Mr. Bennett- Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 2-Powers of commission.

Before the recess the Prime Minister spoke at some length with regard to this measure, and to two or three statements which my right hon. friend has been making from time to time I should like to take very strong exception, in the hope that he will not repeat them.
The first statement is that anyone on this side of the house is in any way seeking to prejudice public ownership either in the minds of hon. members of this house or of the public generally. May I tell the Prime Minister that it was a Liberal administration that appointed the royal commission that brought in the report on radio broadcasting, recommending that this service be made a government owned and operated utility The Liberal party has taken its stand strongly behind 
that proposal, and we are just as anxious as the Prime Minister and hon. gentlemen opposite to see this government owned utility made a success and secure the confidence of the public. Indeed we are wholeheartedly in favour of government ownership and control of radio broadcasting. Any criticisms we may have to make from this side are directed not against public ownership as Such but rather in an endeavour to remove those features which may tend to create prejudice against government ownership as it exists under the present radio broadcasting commission. When the right hon. gentleman speaks about private interests getting succor and support from those who are bringing forward criticisms with respect to any features of the present commission, let me say that he is simply drawing a herring across the trail. There can be no question as to the motives behind the criticisms which we have been making from this side.
The Prime Minister said the choice was between having radio 'broadcasting under a commission or under a government department, and he went on to say that if it were under a government department it would become a political machine. I think the Prime Minister is quite wrong. I do not think he would admit for a moment that the post office, which is a public utility, is a political machine. Though there may be reasons for so regarding it at the present time, I do not think he would admit that his own Department of External Affairs, which is a department of government, is a political machine.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not a business.

But the post office is a business and there is a great deal in connection with the departments of Maxine, Fisheries, Public Works, Trade and Commerce and other departments of government that has to do with business. They have not become political machines because of the fact that appointments to the public service are made through the instrumentality of the Civil Service Commission. The absence of this protection is the feature to which we are taking exception in the bill my right hon. friend is now proposing. He Is taking the appointments under the radio broadcasting commission out from under the control of the Civil Service Commission, which has been the one body that has saved our government departments so far as appointments to their staffs are concerned from becoming purely political machines. Some degree of censorship will undoubtedly be expected by the country and will

Radio Broadcasting Act
be approved by hon. members, but great care will have to be exercised as to how that censorship is to be enforced, and as to the judgment and discretion with which it is to be exercised. So far as censorship goes, that is the extent of our criticism. As regards the appointment of staffs however the Prime Minister has told the house that there are certain appointments which Mr. Gladstone Murray says should be made by the radio commission itself. Well, no one is contending that the radio commission should have to go to the Civil Service Commission before its members can employ artists or highly technical or professional persons or others necessary to fill the parts essential to any broadcast. All we are asking at the moment is that with respect to the great body of officers, clerks and employees generally, these classes shall be appointed in the same way as others are appointed who are doing similar classes of work in the public service. There is a very strong reason for that with regard to the public service of Canada generally. If we are to leave to different commissions the right to determine what salaries are to be paid for certain classes of work, there will be endless friction between employees in the public service in and under the various departments of government. The Civil Service Commission was established amongst other reasons for the purpose of classifying certain kinds of work and attaching to the different classifications the salaries that seemed to be appropriate.
A few weeks ago we removed from the purview of the Civil Service Commission many appointees on the staffs of the penitentiaries, leaving to the chief of the penitentiaries staff the appointment of persons connected with the institution and the salaries to be attached to those positions. With respect to the railways we took away from parliament the authority to determine the salaries to be paid in different branches of that service, leaving that function to a group of trustees. And with respect to the tariff board, the government has removed from the Civil Service Commission the duty of appointing the staff of that board and of fixing their salaries. In respect of other bodies the same thing has been done, with the reservation in one or two cases that the governor in council must approve the salaries. Here however there is no approval of salaries demanded. We shall soon have throughout the public service as many rates of salaries as there are commissions and bodies of the kind. The Civil Service Commission exists to prevent that sort of thing and to see that throughout
the public service those employees performing similar services should receive similar rates of pay.
That is what we ask at the moment with respect to these employees, and I do say that unless that control is preserved by the Civil Service Commission the government will be making a grave mistake and will certainly be converting the radio broadcasting commission into a political machine. I think the Prime Minister himself must feel that what I have suggested by way of amendment is fair. Let me read the amendment I propose to offer to section 1 if my right hon. friend will not see his way to accepting it:
To strike out the words "and other officers, clerks and employees or other" in lines 6 and 7, and to insert the word "and" after the word "technical" in line 6.
The section as amended would then read:
The commission may employ such technical and professional persons as the commission may deem necessary or desirable, and such persons shall receive such salaries or remuneration as may be fixed by the commission.
That makes it clear that so far as all technical and professional persons are concerned -and both these words may be construed in a very broad sense to include artists and persons of special talent-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The statute in another clause is clear in that respect.

Then, so far as these classes are concerned, we are prepared, with the proviso which the Prime Minister says he is prepared to make, of having the provisions of the bill apply only until March of next year, to have such persons appointed by the radio commission. I do not think it would be right, however, especially if it is desired to establish public confidence in the commission, that stenographers, clerks and others of the radio commission staff doing administrative work generally, and work corresponding exactly to what many of them have been doing up to the moment, should be made exceptions of by being separated from that control which the Civil Service Commission exercises over similar classes of employees in the public service.

When the bill creating the radio commission came before the house last year I objected to it. I did not speak against it, contenting myself with expressing my opposition by vote. I did not speak against it because I was in such a hopeless minority that I realized that any objections I might raise would be laughed at as groundless fears. My objections to the nationalizing of radio were quite simple. I am opposed to any ex-
Radio Broadcasting Act

tension of the activities of government in the realm of business or over the lives or activities of our people. I am opposed to any further building up of bureaucracy which might seek to control all the activities of this country. We are gradually building up such a bureaucracy, and if we continue the time will come when all aspiring people in the country will look to the government or to some political party for advancement in life. That is not in the public interest. Any advantage we might reap-I say might-from public ownership or control of common utilities would be far more than offset by the disadvantage of having people all depending on governments.
I also object to having any commission arranging for me the programs which I shall listen to over the radio. I prefer to choose my own programs. If I cannot tune in on one station I want to be free to time in on another, and I do not want any commission dictating what it shall be.
I also feared, at the time the bill was introduced, that the licence fee would be raised. It was raised. It was doubled, and I understand it would have been redoubled had the opportunity been favourable. I am told that the commission would like to have raised it still higher, but they thought the time was not opportune because people were hard up; but they are looking forward to the time when they can raise it still higher.
I will not repeat the arguments advanced this afternoon from this side in opposition to censorship. I am thoroughly opposed to it, as were the speakers this afternoon. But in regard to the argument that we must have a national broadcasting system in order to build up a Canadian spirit, because our people were apt to lose their patriotism owing to the influence of foreign programs-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was not stated.

It was not stated in those words, but it has been said that in order to build up a Canadian spirit-we will put it that way-it is necessary to have true Canadian programs. Let us look at the rules and regulations of the broadcasting commission and see what they regard as truly Canadian programs:
A program of foreign origin which advertises goods manufactured in Canada and names the address in this country where such goods are produced and distributed shall be deemed a Canadian program.
In other words, a program can be produced one hundred per cent in Chicago and so long as it advertises Canadian goods it shall be deemed a Canadian program. If the programs

we were getting from abroad were going to make us all Yankees instead of Canadians, I do not see anything in this regulation that will change that. Such programs can still come in provided they advertise Canadian goods. It seems to me that the same hand that was at work devising these rules and regulations was also at work devising the customs rates, and the regulations are designed not to shut out the ballyhoo of the Yankee but rather to prevent us from listening to his advertising. The fear is not that we shall import American ideas but that we shall import some American goods. The greatest objection I have to the commission is in connection with the unethical practices to which they have resorted in order to beat out their competitors. Any merchant who tried to beat out his competitor not by giving better value or better service to his customer but by overturning his competitor's delivery van and spoiling his goods would be considered unethical and be despised and condemned by every right thinking person in the country. That is precisely what this commission has done. When the bill went through last year I thought that if we did not like their programs we would be able to tune in on the American stations as we had done in the past. However, we now find that we cannot tune in on any of those stations. The commission has so arranged the wave lengths as to make this impossible. In my opinion, this is unethical and should be condemned in the strongest terms.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The suggested amendment of the right hon. the leader of the opposition does not meet the difficulty to whioh attention has been directed. It is felt that the words "and other officers" should at least remain in to be dealt with by the commission. I am quite content to have the section amended to read as follows:
The commission may employ such technical, professional and other officers as the commission may deem necessary or desirable, and such persons shall receive such salaries or remuneration as may be fixed by the commission.
There will then be added these words:
Clerks and all other employees of the commission shall be appointed pursuant to the Civil Service Act.
The only distinct difference between us is as to whether other officers shall be appointed by the commission or by the Civil Service Commission. It was that difficulty that influenced me in suggesting that it should be only for a limited time. There was an inability to settle definitely upon what would constitute other officers. This could not be done without a great deal of study being given to the matter, more than the Civil

Service Commission was in position to give up to this time. May I remind the committee that in dealing with the National Research Council my right hon. friend appointed a head to that body for a period of five or seven years and inaugurated a line of salaries which were out of line with those paid in the civil service. This caused a great deal of heartburning and some differences and difficulties which we are endeavouring to adjust.
I quite follow every argument which has been used as to the undesirability of having different salaries paid by different commissions for the same services but there is at once the answer suggested in connection with the National Research Council, namely, that the struggle to get a certain type of qualified persons is such in view of competition that you must pay the going salaries for the workers required. As I Say, I desire to meet in every way in my power the suggestions which have been made, but I think the whole purpose would fail if the words "and other officers" were stricken out and these employees made subject to the Civil Service Commission. That commission is not able to deal with that phase of the matter and the radio commission must be in a position to do so if it is to function. I believe that because it is what they tell me positively. _
Mr. Murray is very clear about it. I do not desire to quote him again but he has stated that if we are to make this succeed, we should take this course. I should like to endeavour to assist those who are trying to do it.

A half loaf

I suggest this simply because I think the Prime Minister himself sees the wisdom of not having different salaries paid in the public service for similar classes of work. If the salaries to be paid these professional, technical and other officers were required to have the approval of the governor in council, I think there would be a greater probability of uniformity in the salaries paid throughout the public service. I suggest to my right hon. friend the addition of those words to the amendment he himself is proposing.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved the second reading of Bill No. 106, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this house will recall that at the beginning of the session an endeavour was made completely to revise and consolidate the Canada Shipping Act, and a bill was introduced in the Senate for that purpose. When that bill was under consideration by the Senate committee on banking and commerce, however, it developed that there might be some question as to Canada's power to enact all the legislation therein contemplated, and after a very full discussion the bill was withdrawn. During the hearing before the committee, however, it was made apparent that some remedial legislation should be enacted in order to protect our Canadian shipowners, and that some amendments should be made to our coasting laws.
The primary object of this bill is to amend our coasting laws in order to put them on a parity with the laws of the United States. Under section 935 of our present act United States bottoms cannot transport goods or passengers directly from one Canadian port to another Canadian port, but the law is evaded by taking goods from a Canadian to a United States port, let us say from Fort William to Buffalo, where a transshipment is made to another United States ship which takes the goods to Montreal. The United States ships do indirectly what is forbidden under section 935 of the Canada Shipping Act.
Has the minister any information as to the volume of that business?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I will give that information when we get in committee, when I will have all the statistics with regard to this traffic. We are trying now to make our laws exactly the same as those of the United

Canada Shipping Act
States; as a matter of fact the wording is about the same. At present section 935 reads as follows:
No goods or passengers shall be carried by water, from one port of Canada to another, except in British ships.
2. If any goods or passengers are so carried, contrary to this part, the master of the ship or vessel so carrying them shall incur a penalty of four hundred dollars; and any goods so carried shall be forfeited, as smuggled.
The amendment suggested in the present bill will read as follows:
No goods shall be transported by water or by land and water, from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, either directly or by way of a foreign port, or for any part of the transportation in any ship other than a British ship.
2. No ship other than a British ship shall transport passengers from one place in Canada to another place in Canada either directly or by way of a foreign port.
And so on. In order to illustrate my point I will read the existing law in the United States, under which foreign vessels are debarred from participation in the United States coasting trade directly or indirectly:
No merchandise shall be transported by water under penalty of forfeiture thereof from one port of the United States to another port of the United States, either directly or via a foreign port, or for any part of the voyage, in any other vessel than a vessel of the United States.
We have been asked by those interested to enact the same law for the protection of Canadian and British bottoms.
Who are those interested?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Every Canadian should be interested because this is for the protection of our own people.
Did every Canadian ask for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The majority of
Canadians are asking for it. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that when this matter was before the Senate committee many people were heard on that very point, and those opposed to this amendment have failed to make a case. They only had a fear that rates might be increased between Fort William or any other port in Canada and Montreal or other Canadian ports. I think it has been made abundantly clear that there is nothing to fear in that respect. We have plenty of Canadian bottoms to transport goods and passengers between Canadian ports either directly or indirectly, so there is no danger of rates being increased. As this house knows, the rates are under the control of the Board of Grain Commissioners. They regulate the rates. Moreover, under section 938 of the act the governor in council has power-
Is there not a maximum rate which the grain commission may fix? Is there not protection in it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There is ample protection in it. In the event of any undue increase in rates owing to lack of competition or for other reasons, the governor in council has power to suspend any clauses of this statute. Section 938 provides that:
The governor in council may from time to time by order in council declare that the "foregoing provisions" of this part shall not, for the period specified in such order in council apply, either throughout Canada or in any specified waters of Canada, to the ships or vessels, or to any specified, ascertained, or ascertainable class or number of the ships or vessels, of any foreign country.
We are therefore protected. Those who had any fears in the matter were reassured; it was proved clearly to them that they were protected in three ways.
How long has the governor it council had that power?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Since 1923. Those interested in shipping grain or any other commodities are protected in three ways, by fair competition, by the regulations of the grain board, and by section 938 of the statute. I think it is only fair that our Canadian bottoms should enjoy the same protection as American bottoms in our waters.
There are other small amendments. They are not very important but we have taken the opportunity to include them in this bill. First, there is an amendment with respect to authority in the matter of pilotage. So far the authority has been vested in the Minister of Marine, but we have deemed it wise to substitute for the amendment proposed in the bill one providing that the authority vested in the minister in pilotage matters shall be conferred on the deputy minister in the absence of the minister. For the proper administration of the department I think it wise that this amendment should be accepted. Another amendment has reference to the inspection of ship's tackle for the protection of those engaged in the loading and unloading of vessels in Canadian ports. This amendment conforms with the legislation adopted by the League of Nations international labour bureau last year. This provision serves a very useful purpose for the protection of those employed in loading and unloading ships. Every country that signed the agreement will adopt the same legislation. The next amendment provides that everyone shipping goods weighing over 2,240 pounds shall indicate the weight on the package before it is loaded on the ship. As the result of experience this provision has also been adopted by the League of Nations inter-
Canada Shipping Act

national labour bureau last year for the protection of navigation and seamen. The next amendment requires that helm orders shall be given in the direct sense on all ships registered in Canada. This provision was adopted by the international convention for the safety of life at sea and was ratified by this house by chapter 49 of the session of 1931. Every country is accepting the regulation in order to have uniformity in the direction of ships. I do not think there is anything else I can add at the moment, but when the bill is in committee any information desired will be given.

I have
a few remarks to make with respect to section 935, to which the minister has referred. All members from western Canada are particularly interested in this section because it is possible that if the amendment is put into effect it will have some bearing, directly or indirectly, upon the rates which will be charged' on grain passing over the lakes to eastern ports. I am satisfied that all western members have followed with the keenest interest and have read probably more than once the evidence which was submitted to the standing committee of the Senate on banking and commerce with respect to the original bill, letter J. respecting the Canada Shipping Act. The first witnesses who were heard by that committee were those who appeared on behalf of the grain producers of western Canada. The first witness to appear on behalf of such producers was Mr. P. F. Bredt, representing the Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba pool organizations. Mr. Bredt's view with respect to this particular section is set out at page 44 of the evidence, and possibly I might bring the crux of the amendment to the attention of the house by pointing out that if section 935 becomes law it will mean that only grain carried to Buffalo from Fort William or Port Arthur in Canadian vessels can be transferred to the port of Montreal. The contention of those who appeared on behalf of the various producers was that if this section became law the result would be to create more or less of a monopoly for Canadian shippers with respect to the transfer of grain from Buffalo to Montreal. Mr. Bredt sets forth the view of the three western grain pools in a written memorandum which appears on page 44 of the evidence. This reads:
Whereas the suggested amendment to the Canada Shipping Act would prevent transshipment of Canadian grain through Buffalo or other American lake ports except in Canadian vessels, and
Whereas it is essential in the best interests of Canada that no avenue of outlet for our grain should be closed, and

Whereas the passing of this amendment would result in restrictions of trade through inability to take advantage of possible lower ocean freights at Montreal or Quebec on all Canadian grain stored in lake Erie American ports, and
Whereas it would also have the effect of creating a virtual monopoly on freights to Montreal, which might react seriously against us in the world's markets.
Therefore be it resolved that we, as representatives of a large percentage of western Canadian producers, protest strongly against legislation which will in any way interfere with the normal movement of our grain.
Mr. Bredt stated that those were the views of the three pool associations which were said to have handled approximately forty-five per cent of the crop last year. I note that the minister, speaking in this regard, said something to the effect that those who were protesting against this amendment had not put up a very good case. Dealing with this matter, I note that Mr. Bredt states at page 46:
It is very difficult, of course, to state definitely that it would mean an increase in rates.
On page 51, he gives the following answer to a question asked by the Hon. Mr. Ballan-tyne:
Q. Air. Bredt, if this act went through do you claim it would increase freight rates?
A. There is a danger as we see it, we may be wrong.
While Mr. Bredt expressed the view of the associations in the manner I have quoted, he still seemed to think that there was a certain amount of doubt. The United Grain Growers also filed a memorandum with the committee. Their president was not before the committee personally but he sent a telegram to the chairman, part of which reads as follows:
The principal interest of this to the Canadian grain trade and to the producers of grain in western Canada, including many thousands of shareholders and customers of United Crain Growers on whose behalf this company feels it necessary to speak lies in connection with the Buffalo route for lake transportation of grain and also in the competition in lake freights which the use of that route has made possible
While we recognize that certain conditions in lake transportation have at times driven lake freights on grain down to levels unremunerative to vessel owners and lower than could be maintained for any great length of time, we must point out that the competition from United States vessels has at times in the past been an important factor in holding down lake freights and we fear dangers to the interests of grain producers if such competition is permanently eliminated.
Mr. Sydney Smith, the president of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, also appeared before the committee and his views are set

Canada Shipping Act
forth in the evidence. Mr. Smith stated that he represented the unanimous opinion of the export committee of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, and at page 76 he says:
On behalf of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, which I represent, I should like to say that iny instructions are that they are not at all interested. nor are the export trade particularly interested in forcing grain on any route. The general idea-if I have not explained it clearly, it is my fault-is that they want the freedom of the export routes that now exist, and they believe that that is in the interest of the producer of western Canada. Although the gram exchange has sometimes been accused of being an institution that mixed everything up in connection with grain, they have at least identified themselves with the producer in this.
On page 65 Mr. Smith states that in his opinion this amendment might create a monopoly, but at page 74, in answer to a question by the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, he makes a rather significant statement. Mr. Meighen's question was:
You are not in the shipping business?
Mr. Smith replied:
I am in the export business. I am not talking of any interests in Buffalo, I am talking of the viewpoint in the west, that we should like these two channels left open. We may be loot ing at a bogy, but that is what we think.
Mr, Smith is a man of vast experience in the exporting business. I suppose he is one of the greatest, if not the greatest exporter in Western Canada. He states that they should like these two channels left open, that they may be looking at a bogy but that is what they think. I might point out that in supporting his contention that a monopoly might be created, Mr. Bredt stated that in July last the lake shippers formed an association known as the Associated Lake Freighters, Limited. Mr. Bredt stated that this association came into being on July 10 and that on July 11 the rates were raised, other increases taking place at periods of a few days until the rates were increased from four and a half cents, I think his statement was, to seven cents. A fraction o<f a cent of difference in shipping charges often determines the route by which grain will be shipped, and before I, for one, would be prepared to support this bill, I would certainly have to know, if the shipping interests are to be benefited, that it is not to be at the expense of the producers. The minister may be able to show us by the statistics which he has and as a result of the amendments which are contained in this bill, that the effect will be to give an increased volume of business to Canadian vessels, thus helping them, but certainly I would not for a moment be prepared to support this bill if I thought the effect would be, as I said a moment ago, to increase in the slightest degree, by a fraction of a cent, the cost to the grain producers of the west.
Another element which I think should be cleared up, I presume in committee, is the matter of safeguards or control. The minis-
ter, in the few introductory remarks which he made, referred to control, and read to the house the provisions of section 938 of the Shipping Act. I regret that I did not have an opportunity of reading carefully the provisions of that section, but I was surprised to hear the minister say that it had been in effect since 1923. I of course accept the minister's statement. But lion, members from the west will remember that, I think in 1924 or 1925, I am not sure of the year, there was some trouble with respect to shipping grain east. An hon. member informs me that it was 1922. If 1922 was the year, probably that would account for the amendment in 1923. At that time United States vessels had to be invited in to break our laws and we had to grant them immunity for so doing, which Was a rather paradoxical situation. I should be glad if, when we are an committee, the minister would again read to us the provisions of section 938, so that if that is the case it [DOT]may be made dle,ar to us, that the governor in council may by order in council suspend the provisions of the bill now before us for consideration.
In the evidence to which I have referred the only questions that were asked of Mr. Bredt with respect to control appear on page 56:
Right Hon. Arthur Meighen:	But with
evolution the units get bigger and there has to be control.
Mr. Bredt: That answers the question, then, that we must L^ve a rate control body?
I may say in fairness to Mr. Bredt that he did not express any opinion other than this with respect to the advisability of control.
The minister has referred to the power which at the present time is vested in the Board of Grain Commissioners with respect to control of rates. I have looked up the provisions of the act and I am not so clear in my own mind that the board have sufficient control. While the minister was speaking one member interjected that the act provides for maximum control, which is the case. Section 3 of the Inland Water Freight Rates Act of 1923 provides for the filing with the Board of Grain Commissioners of the tariff of rates to be charged, as well as subsequent changes in that regard. Section 4 of that act provides:
It shall be the duty of the board to receive and tabulate all such tariffs and rates as may be filed with the board as aforesaid, and moreover, to ascertain by all available means, the rates of freight which prevail or are exacted or required for the carriage of grain from Fort William or Port Arthur to any of the ports or places aforesaid, and to consider and report to the Minister of Trade and Commerce from time to time any facts which may come

Canada Shipping Act
to the knowledge of the board and which tend to show that there is a deficiency of cargo space, excessive freight charges or discrimination in the rates with respect to the carriage of grain as aforesaid, and all shipowners and other persons engaged in the grain carrying trade in Canada shall, npon reasonable request, immediately furnish to the board such information as they may possess relating to any of the matters aforesaid, and shall for any wilful refusal or neglect to furnish the same be guilty of an offence against this act and be liable to a penalty recoverable upon summary conviction not exceeding one thousand dollars and not less than two hundred dollars for each such offence.
Section 5, which is the operative part, provides :
When in the opinion of the board the toll, charge or rate which any company, owner or person charges or intends or proposes to charge for the carriage of grain as aforesaid is unreasonable or excessive or amounts to an unjust discrimination against any person, company or class of persons as compared with the tolls or rates for similar traffic between Canadian and United States ports, or between one port and another in either of said countries, the board may prescribe such maximum rates as it may consider reasonable.
The section goes on to provide that the rates so prescribed may be limited in their application to particular seasons of the year.
If there is a possibility of a monopoly being created, or if there is, by reason of the fact that our coastal laws are changed, a possibility of their having the effect which I have previously set out, then it is certainly most important that the government retain complete control so that it may at any time the need arises take action either through the Board of Grain Commissioners or by order in council to keep effective control over the situation. I may say in that connection that Mr. Sydney Smith stated that he did not think it was necessary to have a board but that if the act was left as it was competition would effectively settle the rates. But the fact is that under the old act there did arise in July of last year a situation which those appearing before the board treated as a monopoly, and upon that occasion they appealed to the Board of Grain Commissioners and had a maximum rate fixed. I do not know on how many occasions the Board of Grain Commissioners have acted in that way, but I am ratlier under the impression that there have been only two. Certainly up to the present the board has not been regarded as a rate fixing body.
I have made these remarks, Mr. Speaker, with a view to drawing to the attention of the house certain facts which in a measure cover the situation. Might I again state that in order for this bill to receive my support it will have to be shown to me quite clearly 53719-323i
that there is ample provision for protecting the western producer so that he will not become the victim of any monopoly which may result from the bringing into effect of this amendment; also that there will be effective control, and that if there is to be benefit to those engaged in the carrying of this grain, it shall not be acquired at the expense of the grain grower.

I
was under the impression, Mr. Speaker, that there was a time-honoured rule that speakers should be taken alternatively in an important debate, and I cannot recollect in a rather long experience a cabinet member introducing a bill being immediately followed by a speaker on his own side of the house.
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) was the first to rise to his feet and was first seen by the Speaker when the minister sat down. There was no discrimination in the matter.

I see that Bourinot at page 334 says:
In all important debates it is customary for the Speaker to endeavour to give the preference, alternately, to the known supporters and opponents of a measure or question.
The same rule is followed in this house invariably. But if an hon. member desiring to speak neglects to rise to his feet and another hon. member is on his feet the latter has a right to be heard.

I was on my feet first. I was on my feet too soon, as a matter of fact. However, I am not surprised at all.
We have waited twenty-five years for a measure of this kind, and now a sorry substitute for the reform we desired has been brought down in the very last hours of the session.
I am not rising to deal with the subject matter which entirely engrossed the minister when he introduced the bill and his supporter behind him. I leave that to be dealt with by members on both sides of the house who are far more competent to deal with it than I am, nor shall I follow the hon. member for Dauphin in putting on Hansard a large portion of the records of another house. I would assume that hon. members interested in the subject would have already read that debate. For a few moments I should like to deal with another matter. I wish to enter a protest against this bill which seeks to amend the Canada Shipping Act having to be discussed in committee of the whole house instead of by the special committee appointed for such purposes, namely the committee which deals with marine and fisheries matters.
Canada Shipping Act

We have an illustration of the need for such reference to a committee in the fact that this bill, which I suppose contains a dozen sections, has been referred to as regards one section only. But there are a dozen more sections.
The general character of any bill amending the shipping act is largely technical and for that reason it is all the more necessaiy it should be referred to a committee, because there are very few, if any men, in this house thoroughly versed in shipping terms. I do not know that there are any men in the house thoroughly versed in the technical terms, and moreover there are very few hon. members -I doubt if there are any-directly representative of the shipping interests, more particularly the seamen, the masters, mates and so on. Therefore a very large body of hon. members will be more or less indifferent to a measure of this type, although it has tonight a special interest given to it because of reference which has been made to the grain trade. The presentation of the bill in this way will mean one of two things, either that it will be a long time going through committee of the whole, or it will go through without being properly understood and debated. A very fine illustration of the advisability of sending it to a committee was seen the other day when one of the most contentious bills -not contentious in a party sense; I refer to the pensions bill-was put through the house in two or three hours, because it-had been thoroughly discussed and agreed to in committee. That is what should be done in this case. May I give an illustration of one or two of the technical points involved. I wonder how many hon. members understand some of the terms with which we will have to deal. I wonder if the minister himself understands them? Does he know what a cotter pin is? Does he know what mousings are? Does he know what a full line is, or a hatch combing, or a heel block, or a hog lashing? I have picked out only one or two at random. Yet we are supposed to discuss the technical use of these terms.
I refer more particularly of course to the big bill which was introduced earlier in the session in the Senate. It contained over eight hundred sections. I am told it was the biggest bill that had ever been introduced into this parliament, and yet it was solemnly proposed, in the face of protest, to bring it into committee of the whole in this house and have it passed in a way which would make it impossible to get anything like appropriate information or discussion on the matter.

Let me quote a sentence or two from letters I have received concerning this bill. In a letter from the Canadian Merchant Service Guild I find the following:
There is no language which we would care to employ that could adequately express the feelings of the masters and officers on this coast with regard to some of the proposals which are contained in the act. When we say that it is rank discrimination that, in our opinion, is only half expressing the situation.
And later:
It is the most impracticable piece of legislation that we have heard of and those who are responsible for framing the act can have little or no practical knowledge of the steamship business, particularly as it affects this coast.
Then the Canadian Association of Seamen, Vancouver branch, writes as follows:
For three weeks we have had a committee working steadily on each clause.
And then they go on to express their opinion about the legislation. The committee worked for three weeks on it, and then they obtained only a vague grasp of it. Then, I should like to make some comments concerning the number of amendments arising from their investigations. The first body I mentioned produced amendments numbering twenty-five. Another body, the All-Canadian Congress, produced twenty-five amendments. Then, the Association of Seamen, which had a committee silting for three weeks, produced amendments which cover many pages. Their amendments are contained on thirty-five closely typewritten pages. After they had sent them in they had another thought, and sent another couple of pages of closely typewritten foolscap containing further amendments and comments they had made concerning the bill. That is the body which has studied the legislation for three weeks. Does that not give some indication of the necessity for this legislation going before a committee where men sitting around the table could take it into consideration, a place where they would have the advantage of the Services of men capable of giving technical explanations? After such treatment they would be in a better position to deal with it.
If I remember correctly, this bill was brought to the house last Saturday. The people on the Pacific coast have not yet heard of it, with the exception of the casual wire which may have been sent out and which could explain only sketchily the nature of the bill Which had been introduced!. As their representatives in this house we are supposed

Canada Shipping Act
to stand up and give competent opinion anid advice on a matter with which we are almost entirely unfamiliar. We have not heard from those men whose interests will be affected.
Is that the famous British justice that we hear so much about? Is it common sense?
Mr. DURANLF.AU: Does the hon. member know that for over a month this bill has been before the Senate?
It was before the Senate, but who in British Columbia knows or wants to know anything about the Senate?

proceedings of the Senate in the newspapers.

It would be a hard day for
us when we had to shape our legislation from newspaper reports, because they cannot be accurate. Besides, did the newspapers wire eight hundred sections? The associations to which I have referred got hold of the big bill, and over forty typewritten pages of proposed changes is the fruit of their research. Those who went through the legislation said it was absurd; they had never seen the like of it. They believed it was the greatest piece of discrimination they had ever seen. But so far as this bill is concerned, I must say that unless it has come to them in their dreams, they have not heard of it. As soon as I got it I mailed it, but I could not wire it. Should we stand here passing something vitally affecting their interests, when they do not know anything about it?
Why was this bill left until the last minute? Why was it not introduced earlier? It has been lying in the minister's office since 1908- I do not blame the minister-but I must say the deputy minister did not have the courage or the enterprise to bring it forward. Then other things developed,-the war, and so on. We have waited all that time. The act was so obsolete that the penalties were described in pounds, shillings and pence, instead of in dollars and cents. It is so obsolete that those who had framed the legislation had never heard of a motor gas boat. During the last two or three years I have begged the minister, time and time again-and I begged the last administration-to bring in a bill and let it stand over for a session thereby giving the people interested an opportunity for discussion.
I shall not take further time of the house. I do hope the government will take notice of what I have said concerning what these people think and want. They are an important body. When the big bill comes down next year it should be sent to a committee. There
are some changes I should like to suggest in this bill, I shall refer to one change made by the 'Senate which in my view is most unfair. It deals with the tackle for the loading and unloading of ships. However I shall speak in committee, and shall give other hon. members who are vitally interested an opportunity to speak now on the motion for second reading.

I rise to oppose the second reading of the bill. As an illustration of legislation calculated to serve special interests, this is about the finest specimen that has come to my attention. I ask the government this question: What was the special hurry in connection with these sections? They constitute only a few out of the very large bill which has to be considered next year. What is the hurry in connection with this bill? The present coastal laws with respect to the great lakes and to the Pacific have remained on our statute books for some time. From time to time they have been altered or amended by order in council and regulation. Now, on the second to the last day of this session, as some of us hope, this bill is suddenly thrust upon us without any opportunity of considering it in a standing committee of the commons. Indeed, in its very make-up there is evidence of the haste with whioh it was drafted, in spite of the consideration given by the Senate committee. I wonder if hon. members of the committee have taken the trouble to read section 3, which appears on page 1 of the bill. Let me read the first three lines:
Whenever the minister is so appointed as the pilotage authority his appointment shall, without, more, extend to his successors in office-
In the name of goodness what does that mean? I have always understood that the language of seamen was a weird and awful thing, and this may have been drafted by a seaman. I understand that when they are ashore "more" is a popular word with them.

imagine so; I should be very much surprised if the minister did not move an amendment. I am not criticizing his proposal to amend the section; I am pointing to the evidence of haste and carelessness which appears in the bill before me.
