Why discuss the
clause now when it is to be amended?

Because it is a typical illustration of the haste in this matter which, as the minister said, is to give protection to special shipping interests. The minister's own words come back to him; this is to give special privilege to some shipping interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
To Canadian ship
owners.

Yes, but how does the minister know they are Canadian companies? When we are in committee of the whole will he be prepared to lay before the committee the names and nationality of the shareholders and the amount of their holdings in these companies? There are many so called Canadian companies that are by no means Canadian, and I should like further information before I accept the glib reference of the minister to Canadian companies.
That is aside from the subject, however; the minister draws these remarks upon himself by his interjections. He has stated that this bill is for the purpose of protecting shipowners, and there is no doubt in my mind that this is the purpose. Equally there is no doubt that this protection will be secured to the disadvantage of the farmers of western Canada.
No.

Yes, that
is my conviction. I will tell the Minister of Marine, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), that it was recognition of the danger of agreements between the two railway companies against the interests of the western grain growers that induced this 'house to put on the statute books a statutory maximum rate for grain moving over the railways. I say that in this case also, if the government are sincere in their desire to protect the interests of the farmers, they will provide a statutory rate on the great lakes for grain and grain products as they have done on the railways.
There is no doubt whatever that section 935 of the bill before us strengthens the position of the lake shippers' association to which the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) very properly referred as having taken advantage of their organized position m days gone by, to the disadvantage of the grain growers of western Canada as well 
as the exporters of grain. Here there are two great interests involved, and it is not going to satisfy the farmers of western Canada to say that the shippers of eastern Canada are to receive a special privilege which enables them to create a monopoly under the guise of legislation, and so take advantage of their position as they did in the past. The hon. member for Dauphin said that representatives of some bodies appearing before the Senate committee feared the possibility of a combine. I say they would have been justified in declaring that it is virtually certain that a combine will be created as soon as this legislation is passed. Indeed, to all intents and purposes there is a monopoly and a combine on the great lakes at the present time. As an illustration of that statement let me remind the committee that last year in spite of steadily declining grain prices to a point which the government must admit to have been far below the cost of production, these lake shippers reorganized their association which apparently had not been operative since the scandal in connection with the previous combine, and at once advanced the rate to 7 cents.
Then this Inland Water Freight Rates Act of 1923 appeared on the scene, but I direct the attention of the government to the fact that here, as in previous cases, no rate fixing power is vested in the Board of Grain Commissioners under the act. Whatever rights they have are ambiguous in the act, and it is questionable whether or not the act is within the competence of this parliament. At any rate, according to all the information I have been able to secure, no decisions have been handed down as such by the Board of Grain Commissioners under the Inland Water Freight Rates Act of 1923, but they brought moral pressure, moral suasion, to bear on the lake shippers. The result has been that in spite of the collapse in grain prices we secured a reduction of only half a cent in the freight rates on the great lakes, a reduction from 7 to 6J cents.
I can assure the members of the government that the farmers of the west do not look upon that sort of protection as at all adequate. As soon as this body is created the farmers will pay the price to the shareholders of these companies. I submit that instead of going into this thing in this way-I am reminded by a good friend of mine that the promise of some reciprocal trade treaty with the United States looms on the horizon -the government should delay action on this bill. The matter is not so very urgent, so why not delay action until the complete re-

Canada Shipping Act
vision takes place next year, and in the meantime the government might exert all its influence in order to secure a cooperative agreement with the United States so as to free shipping on the great lakes and give the farmers healthy competition in regard to rates. Some hon. gentlemen may argue that the farmer does not get the benefit of reduced rates on the great lakes, and I think that is very true. I believe that in the majority of cases when there is a temporary reduction, especially in the shipping season, say a monthly or a weekly reduction, it is the exporter who gets the advantage. I do not think there is any doubt about it; the man who owns the grain at Fort William gets the benefit. I ask hon. gentlemen to notice that the creation of the pools, especially when they established their own agencies at Liverpool, brought into the picture an entirely new factor so that the farmers were enabled to secure the advantages of the reduced rates because of the fact that they were themselves shipping grain and selling it on the Liverpool market.
There is a further point in this connection which should not escape hon. gentlemen; it is that when the rates are pushed up at once the farmer is compelled to carry the load. The increase is deducted from the Fort William price, and this is a factor in determining the level of wheat prices in Winnipeg and throughout the west. So any bill of this kind, which is calculated to create a monopoly unless accompanied by a statutory maximum rate, does not do justice to the farmers of the west, and in my opinion should not be permitted to pass the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Garland, Bow River) asked the reason for the hurry with this bill, and suggested that it should be left over until next year. There is at least one veiy good reason, if not several. It will be recalled that for some time past- and personally I have had the matter in hand for several years-pressure has been brought to bear upon the government to enact some safety legislation with regard to ships' tackle and so forth. But those who were urging this were advised that the revision of the shipping act was coming forward in the near future, and it was suggested .that they should wait until that time arrived. This year an attempt was made to introduce a complete revision of the shipping act, but certain very serious constitutional difficulties arising out of the necessity of synchronizing the new revised act with the statute of Westminster and
similar shipping acts throughout other parts of the empire made it necessary to postpone the revision. It was thought desirable therefore to bring in this brief bill for the purpose at least of giving effect to .this safety appliance provision with regard to ships' tackle. That is one reason, and to my mind a sufficient reason, and I wish to pay due meed of praise to .my colleague for bringing this forward and doing a measure of justice to those who are engaged in the hazardous work of loading ships in our various ports. It has been recognized for a long time that such hazardous work called for some definite measures .that would reasonably protect the workmen while at their task, and before turning may attention to the controversial clause of the bill I should like to refer briefly to that portion of it.
The hon. member for Comox-Aiberni (Mr. Neill), in his usual sarcastic manner,-
Thank you.

-referred to this part of the bill in most scathing berms. I think his remarks were entirely unjustifiable. There is nothing mysterious about the nautical or shipping terms used in the bill; they are ordinary terms which are quite common and are fully understood tooth by the officials dealing with the matter and by any person who has had any acquaintance with shipping, and most certainly by everyone associated with the work of seamen. But there is no reason why my hon. friend should sneer at the supposed ignorance of members of the government so far as these nautical .terms are concerned. The hon. gentleman .is not .the only man in the house or in the world who has a fairly wide knowledge of many of these things, and I would suggest to him that he would have been serving those whose interests he frequently pretends .to have at heart-
Order.

There is nothing out of
order in that. I say, he would have been serving much better those whose interests he has at heart had he said a word of commendation to the minister for at least the attempt to bring in these measures providing for safety appliances in the ports. In regard to that feature of the bill I would say this- details of course will be discussed in committee ; I am making a very brief reference to the matter here. Provision will be made for an inspector in the ports, to be paid by the government or by the port authorities, to inspect ship's tackle. It is commonly known that frequently stevedoring companies in loading ships will put a more severe strain upon
Canada Shipping Act

the tackle than it is properly constructed to bear, and so in the bill it is provided that when any heavy weights are to be loaded, weights such as heavy machinery, huge castings, and things of that kind, the weight if above a specified point must be clearly marked on the article itself, and due care must be taken in the handling of such heavy weights. Furthermore, the inspector is empowered to enter a ship at any time and demand access to its tackle, and any information, any records or matters of that description that may be required by him in the inspection of tackle to see that it is safe shall be provided. He is also empowered to see that any man working around ships at night shall do so by adequate lighting. He is empowered, again, where he learns of a practice which is becoming very common, of having men working in the hold of ships when huge weights are being lowered, in the larger ships from a comparatively great height, to see that the men are not forced to work under conditions such as they have worked under in the past. I know, as I am sure my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni also knows, that particularly on the Pacific coast where large fir logs, huge things weighing tons, are loaded to be shipped to Japan, frequently serious accidents occur and sometimes death because men have been compelled by shall I say rather avaricious bosses to work in dangerous situations. The minister and his staff have provided in this bill very fair and adequate measures for the protection of such men, and I submit that if for no other reason at all the bill should be welcomed by -the house. It ought to be having the support to-night of members who are not in the house and who ought to be in their places to support it. There is another provision dealing with pilotage, with which I am not so familiar, but which I understand is desirable in the interests of the pilotage authorities of the country.
Now, for these purposes the bill was justified in its introduction into this house. In the closing clause of the bill will be noted a paragraph which I think is absolutely necessary because of the new conditions which arise out of the passage of the statute of Westminster.
I am not presuming now to give any opinion from a legal standpoint, for I am not competent to do so; I merely state the matter as a layman. I understand however that by the passage of the statute of Westminster there are certain provisions of the Canadian act which if disturbed now might be regarded as not in harmony with the statute of West-
minster and the old act, and so it was necessary to insert this clause, closing the bill:
No provision of this act shall be deemed to operate as a repeal within the meaning or pursuant to the provisions of the statute of Westminster, 1931, or otherwise, of any provision of ,the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894, of the parliament of Great Britain, or any amendment thereof or addition thereto.
The need for that is that until the Canada Shipping Act is completely revised and brought into complete harmony with the act of Westminster it is imperative that we maintain all rights which shipping interests, sailors, masters and others have under both the Canada Shipping Act and the Merchant Shipping Act, both of which statutes are largely interwoven in their administration in Canada. This is an added reason why the bill should go through now.
May I turn now briefly to the controversial clause of the bill, the amendment to section 935 of the Canada Shipping Act? The hon. member for Bow River a moment ago, with that vigour for which he is so noted, and that eloquence that marks all his utterances, declared that this legislation was designed to create a monopoly in shipping. He said it was designed to serve special interests, the shipping interests, and he also said we had designed the legislation to serve such special interests because we wished to injure the producer. That is summing up very briefly the observations of the hon. gentleman, and I may say that in making these observations he has voiced an opinion which I have heard expressed in the last few days in casual conversation by some who apparently have not given due consideration to the proposals contained in this bill.
I submit in the first place that the bill is not designed for any such purpose; but there is a certain condition obtaining in Canada which has obtained for many years to which it is desirable the Canadian parliament should give consideration. I shall give certain figures in a moment to support my point, but briefly stated it is this: so far as the movement of American grain from American ports to the seaboard is concerned, Canadian ships cannot get any share of that business. Let us put that down clearly as a statement of fact. We are not complaining about it; that is the business of our American neighbours, but under their law Canadian ships cannot share in that or any other business. For the moment, we are dealing largely with grain. On the other hand, Canadian grain or other merchandise

Canada Shipping Act
which moves in large quantities from the head of the lakes may be and has been moved quite freely by American vessels. It has moved just as freely and in almost as large quantities as by Canadian vessels. While hon. gentlemen may feel some apprehension should we attempt to divert a larger portion of this particular trade to Canadian bottoms, I submit that it is certainly no crime for the Canadian parliament, this government, myself or anyone else to propose to nurture Canadian shipping interests. It is no greater crime than proposing that we should nurture Canadian interests in any other branch of activity.

The minister says that at the present time Canadian grain can be moved and is being moved practically as freely by American bottoms from Canadian ports to seaboard as in Canadian boats. Could that be done from one Canadian port to another?

If my hon. friend will bear with me while I make a general argument, I will come back and demonstrate that point in a moment. Let us lay this down as being fair at least: it is the business of parliament to nurture Canadian interests, whatever those interests may be. In this instance we have found that Canadian shipping interests on the great lakes are subject to a discrimination. As I have stated already, they are precluded from sharing in the business from American sources but they must share the Canadian business with American bottoms. Let us examine this briefly. Then we come to the grain moved to Buffalo by American boats where it goes into storage. The voyage is ended as far as we are concerned. Buffalo is a sort of kicking-off place; the grain may go to New York, to Baltimore, to Portland, to Boston or to Montreal and, to a lesser degree, to Halifax or Saint John during the winter time. However, that is a movement by rail and does not concern us at this time. The fact is that the shipment ends at Buffalo and becomes a new shipment when it goes on to Montreal. American boats are allowed to go in to pick up this grain and move it to Montreal. This cannot be done under the American law with the conditions reversed.
Where would such a reverse condition prevail?

There might be a movement from Duluth to lake ports, although nothing like as large as far as grain is concerned. There might be a considerable movement in other commodities. Grain might be moved from Duluth or Chicago to Port Col-borne, to Midland or other ports and from there moved on to Montreal.
On grain moved from Buffalo to Montreal, could you get the preference?

Yes, if that grain is
shipped on a through bill of lading from the head of the lakes, it would get the preference just the same as if it went direct to Montreal.

I do not think the minister grasped my question. I wanted to know where a condition prevails where United States goods come from a United States port to a Canadian port and then back again into the United States.

Has the minister any figures in regard to that?

I have them somewhere,
but I cannot lay my hands on them at the moment. The movement of course, is very much smaller on the Canadian side. It is not a large movement, but the principle is there just the same that you cannot move United States grain by Canadian vessels to a Canadian port where it is again moved back into United States channels.
In the evidence submitted before the Senate committee, was it not proven that very little, if any, of the grain going from Buffalo back to Montreal ever went out in United States bottoms?
No.
The evidence says so.

My information is-and

From Buffalo to Montreal?

From Buffalo to Montreal, and I gave the name of one of the large shipping companies which handles most of it. I think we are clear, however, on that discrepancy between, shall I say the rights of Canadian shipping interests on the lakes as against United States shipping interests.

In order that we may be
clear on that point, is the minister prepared to assert that the United States laws would prevent Canadian ships from taking United States grain from Port Colborne back to a United States port?
No.
That is a parallel case.

No, I say that a Canadian shipper cannot carry United States grain from a United States port to a Canadian port and
then by the same or another vessel, either one or the other, carry it from that Canadian port back into a United States port. Furthermore, they cannot do that for either leg of the movement. That is why in this bill, as will be noted, the minister has provided:
No goods shall be transported by water or by land and water, from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, either directly or by way of a foreign port, or for any part of the transportation in any ship other than a British ship.
That is why that provision is inserted. That brings us into conformity with the United States law in a reverse situation. I have under my hand the United States law which I might read at this point in juxtaposition with the clause I have read from the present bill:
No merchandise shall be transported by water, under penalty of forfeiture thereof, from one port of the United States to another port of the United States, either directly or via a foreign port, or for any part of the voyage, in any other vessel than a vessel of the United States.
That is the United States law and It will be seen that the legislation we are now enacting is practically the same.
At the present time no United States bottom can take Canadian wheat from one Canadian port to another.

Might I ask one more question purely for the sake of accuracy? As I understand the matter, when this bill becomes law, under the laws of the two countries it will no longer be possible for Canadian grain to go to Buffalo or another United States port and then back to a Canadian port, by any line whatever?
By Canadian vessels.
By either. The United States law would prevent its being done by a Canadian vessel. Wheat having once been shipped from a Canadian port to Buffalo could not be reshipped to a Canadian port.

When we are chided as we were a moment ago by the hon. member for Bow River with not having done any better last year than fixing the maximum rate at 61 cents, it is not quite fair criticism in the light of the rates that have prevailed during all those years. That brings me to the point of control.
My hon. friend from Dauphin and others have asked, is there any effective control? Some slighting remarks were made about the Inland Water Freight Rates Act. I think that was not wisely done. The Inland Water Freight Rates Act, it is true, does not say that the Board of Grain Commissioners shall fix rates at which cargoes shall be moved, in the way that the railway board fixes rates for rail traffic, and there are obvious reasons why that would be undesirable. I think it would be equally inimical to the producers and shippers as well as to others because the board might even fix a rate which was above that which the boats would charge under open competition. There is open competition at the present time. There is not a monopoly on the great lakes; let us get that clear. Many boats are handling grain to-day below the maximum rate fixed. The maximum rate was fixed here about two weeks ago when the matter was referred to me by the chairman of the Board of Grain Commissioners. The board under the act brought the matter to my attention as a matter of routine and a maximum rate was fixed from the head of the lakes to Montreal, Sorel and Quebec of 6| cents, which is looked upon as a fair and equitable rate. Somebody has said that it was unwise to fix maximum rates, suggesting there was something bad about it. Why, Mr. Speaker, the fixation of a maximum rate, leaving it open for competition to give a rate below the maximum, is obviously better than having a rate fixed by some board of commissioners as has been suggested.
Only to the exporter.
To the producer too.
Would the minister be good enough to bring down to the committee tomorrow morning a copy of the order fixing the maximum rate?

I will have that order brought down. Let me now turn to the Inland Water Freight Rates Act. I may say that I criticized this act pretty severely at the time it was passed. My hon. friend (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) will remember when the late Mr. Low was minister, standing right where I am now standing, when he passed this act.
I will say .you criticized it.

And it had a rather bad effect, I believe. Certainly we did criticize the act. The act has been in force. It has seldom been used, it is true, but it has been held there, as it were, over the shippers, and my hon. friends who are somewhat perturbed in the interests of the producers of the west could have invoked this act at any time, but they have not done so-not that I criticize them for that, but they did not invoke the act when the rates were ten and nine and eight cents. But we are putting it into force. We are exercising federal authority. The act says that every shipper shall immediately after entering into a charter party file with the board the terms of his charter party. That is the first clause. The next clause provides, and I think this clause has value and merit in it:
. It shall be the duty of the board to receive and tabulate all such tariffs.
That is the first duty. The next duty is this, that if the board on examination of the rates find that there is any deficiency of cargo space-I pause there for the purpose of emphasizing a very important point. If there is a deficiency of cargo space as there was in the years that I mentioned a moment ago, the particulars of which are under my hand, then what is done is to invoke the powers under the shipping act and suspend the coastwise laws. The clause was read by the Minister of Marine, but I shall read it again. It is section 938 of the Canada Shipping Act:
The governor in council may, from time to time, by order in council declare that the foregoing provisions of this part-
That is the provisions that we are dealing with in this bill, namely sections 935 and other sections:
-shall not, for the period specified in such order in council apply, either throughout Canada or in any specified waters of Canada, to the ships or vessels, or to any specified, ascertained or ascertainable class or number of the ships or vessels, of any foreign country.
That is, the governor in council may admit foreign tonnage into our waters if it is found under this act that there is a shortage of cargo space, and that has been done in almost every year, or in many years at least, during the last ten or twelve or thirteen years. Not only is it to be done in .that case, but should there be any monopoly, should there be any challenge of the right of the government or of the Board of Grain Commissioners under this act to fix a maximum rate, this would then be applied. It has been the practice of governments to do it. It was done many times in the past, repeatedly done, and it is there for us to do it.
Canada Shipping Act

Should that not be considered sufficient, we have a regulation or a clause in the Customs Act, clause 298, which provides:
The governor in council may, from time to time, make regulations for declaring what shall be coasting trade or inland navigation respectively, and how the same shall be regulated in any case or class of cases, and may declare any trade or voyage on the seas, rivers, lakes or waters within or adjacent to Canada, whether to or from any place within or without Canada, or whether such seas, rivers, lakes or waters are or are not geographically, or for the purpose of other acts or laws, inland waters, to be a coasting trade or a coasting voyage within the meaning of this act and of such regulations, any may also, from time to time, by regulation, dispense, on any condition which he sees fit to impose, with such of the requirements of this act as he deems it inexpedient to enforce with regard to vessels engaged in any such trade or with respect to any case or class of cases.
In other words, under the Customs Act the governor in council has power to admit foreign vessels into the coastwise trade, both at sea, inland and elsewhere. So I submit to the committee that there is ample protection against a possible monopoly or against a violation of the principles of this bill.
I have taken more time than I expected, Mr. Speaker, largely because I have tried to answer questions at this stage instead of in committee. Let me conclude with just one or two observations.
Will the shipping interests, someone asks, benefit at the expense of the producer? I submit that that will not be the case. Certainly if I thought for a moment it would, I would never support this bill. I do say that we are entitled to take cognizance of the fact that our 100,000,000 bushels a year is carried in foreign vessels, and we have no opportunity of a like access to the American market. We are entitled to take cognizance af that fact, and to provide regulations which will safeguard Canadian shipping interests. It is not intended, however, that these shipping interests shall take advantage of such a privilege, to the detriment of the producer or shipper. As I have said, ample power is given to us, under the Inland Water Freight Rates Act, in the shipping act and in the Customs Act, to provide against any such encroachments on the rights of shippers, or any danger of a monopoly. Furthermore, such powers have been frequently exercised, and are recognized as common practice in this country.
